topics_text: Pilani Campus ACADEMIC - UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION First Semester 2026-27 Course Handout Part II Date: 31st July 2026 In addition to Part I (General Handout for all courses appended to the Timetable), this portion gives further specific details regarding the course. Course Number: AN F314 Course Title: Introduction to Flight Instructor-in-Charge: Biswadip Shome (biswadip.shome@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Team of Instructors: N/A 1. Course description: This course introduces the fundamental principles governing aircraft flight, including basic aerodynamics, atmospheric properties, aircraft performance, stability and control, propulsion systems, and Hypersonic vehicles. Students explore the forces acting on an aircraft and the engineering concepts that enable safe and efficient flight. The course provides a foundational understanding of flight mechanics and aircraft systems, preparing students for advanced studies in aerospace engineering. 2. Scope and Objective: Following are the scope and objective of this course: a. Understand the fundamentals of flight: Introduce the basic principles of aerodynamics, the four forces of flight, and the physical concepts governing aircraft motion. b. Study aircraft systems and performance: Develop an understanding of aircraft structures, propulsion systems, stability, control, and performance under various operating conditions. c. Apply engineering principles: Use fundamental concepts of mathematics, physics, and engineering to analyse and solve introductory flight-related problems. d. Build a foundation for advanced aerospace studies: Prepare students for higher-level courses in flight mechanics, aircraft design, aerospace propulsion, and aviation engineering. 3. Course Learning Outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, the students will have the following learning outcomes: a. Explain the principles of flight by describing the four fundamental forces (lift, weight, thrust, and drag) and their interactions during flight. b. Analyse atmospheric effects on flight by interpreting how atmospheric properties influence aircraft performance and operations. c. Apply basic aerodynamic concepts to evaluate the performance of airfoil, wings, and aircraft under various flight conditions. Page 1 of 5 Pilani Campus ACADEMIC - UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION d. Evaluate aircraft performance by estimating take-off, climb, cruise, descent, landing, range, and endurance characteristics using fundamental engineering principles. e. Describe aircraft stability and control and explain how control surfaces affect aircraft motion and manoeuvrability. f. Compare aircraft propulsion systems, including propeller- and jet-powered engines, and explain their operating principles and performance characteristics. g. Learn Hypersonic flight, concepts of Newtonian theory and its application to Hypersonic vehicles. h. Solve introductory flight-related engineering problems using mathematics, physics, and computational tools where appropriate. i. Interpret the relationship between aircraft design and flight performance, recognizing how design choices affect efficiency, safety, and operational capability. j. Communicate technical concepts related to flight through written reports, calculations, and engineering discussions 4. Textbooks and Reference Books: TB: J.D. Anderson Jr., Introduction to Flight, 6th Edition, McGraw Hill, 2008. RB: S.K. Ojha, Flight Performance of Aircraft, AIAA Education Series, 1995 5. Method of Conduct of the Course: The course will be conducted using a combination of instructor-centred and learner-centred methods. The former would involve instructor-led class lectures and problem solving exercises while the latter would involve student-led collaborative group projects using simulation for experiential learning, technical report writing, and presentations. 6. Course Outline: Fundamental processes of life at cellular and sub-cellular levels; cell environments; membrane transport; cell movements; division and control mechanisms. 2. Scope and Objective: A fundamental branch in biological sciences, cell biology exposes the learner to the structural and functional organization and working of the cell, the basic unit of life. The field is dynamic and constantly evolving. This course will give an introduction to this branch of biology, by providing experimental data wherever possible. Course Number : BIO F214 Course Title : INTEGRATED BIOLOGY Instructor-in-Charge : Pankaj Kumar Sharma [pankajsharma@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.i pilani.ac.in] Team of Instructor(s) : P. Yadukrishnan [yadukrishnan.p@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in] 1. Course Description: The course intends to bridge the gap and open new vistas to students taking up biology. The course covers two tracks, essentially. The first track introduces the student to the ordering that helps biologists to actually study the vast diversity of the living ing world. This track would encompass questions related to the origin and evolutionary pathways followed in nature, as well as the methods followed by biologists to systematically categorize and document them. The second track highlights the uses and applications applications of biology in everyday life – whether in the economic or in the social realms. Together, the course projects the subject in a way from which the student can choose and implement his biological knowledge vis vis-à-vis his/her interests. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: Being the second course on General Biology, the course exposes the students to the foundational aspects as described above. At the end of the course, the student will have developed a basic understanding of the evolutionary processes, rationale for taxonomic arrangements and familiarity of selected, representative members of the major kingdoms of living organisms. Further, the student will also become aware of how knowledge of biology (both botany and zoology) is applied for benefit of mankind and other organisms. 3. Course Learning Outcomes: a. Course No : BIO F313 Course Title : Animal Physiology Instructor-in-Charge : SHILPI GARG (shilpi@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Instructors : Rajdeep Chowdhury (rajdeep.chowdhury@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Ritobrata Bhattacharyya, Ananya Bhatt 1. Course Description: Basic functional processes in animals; like homeostasis, membrane physiology, digestive, respiratory, excretory, circulatory, reproductive, nervous, sensory, muscular, endocrine systems will be studied at structural, functional, cellular and molecular level. 2. Scope & Objective: This course attempts to bring the awareness among students for major features of animal physiology and co- relate that to the human physiology. Emphasis will be on structure and function relationship and importanc of every organ. In addition, the course will also discuss about some of the diseases that are associated with complication in different organs. 3. Course learning outcomes: a. Integration of multiple organ systems to regulate and maintain homeostasis between the internal and external environments. b. Explore the process of enzymatic digestion and its physiological outcomes within the digestive tract. c. Functional mechanisms of the human kidneys in regulating fluid homeostasis and urine formation. d. Overview of the cardiac cycle, electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation, types of circulatory vessels, regulation of systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and the various cellular components of blood. e. Anatomical and functional organization of nervous system, including its structural and spatial characteristics. f. The role of hormones in regulating homeostasis and supporting essential physiological functions. g. Understanding gas partial pressures, intrapleural pressure dynamics, lung volumes and capacities, respiratory disorders, and the oxygen-carrying capacity of hemoglobin. h. Study of sarcomere structure, the molecular mechanism of muscle contraction, the physiological basis of rigor mortis, and the phenomenon of muscle twitching. i. Exploration of the regulatory mechanisms governing gametogenesis, fertilization, and progression of pregnancy. 5. Text Books: Sherwood, L., Klandorf, H. and Yancey, P.H., Animal Physiology: From Genes to Organisms, 2nd edition, 2013, Brook/Cole Cengage Learning, Singapore Reference Books: Sherwood, L. Principles of Human Physiology, 2007, Brook/Cole Cengage Learning, 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 5. Method of Conduct of the Course The Animal Physiology course will be delivered through a combination of interactive lectures, tutorials (including lab based components during the tutorial hours), and group discussions to promote both conceptual understanding and hands-on experience. Lectures: Core physiological concepts will be taught through structured classroom lectures, supported by visual aids such as diagrams, animations, and clinical case examples to enhance comprehension. Tutorials and Group Discussions: These sessions will focus on clarifying doubts, exploring clinical correlations, and encouraging critical thinking through problem-solving activities and peer interactions. In addition, during some of the tutorial classes, practical sessions will be carried out to examine/ prepare cross- sections of fixed tissues and performing tissue staining to facilitate a detailed understanding of the cross- sectional anatomy of various organs, including the heart and kidney. Assessments: The course will include periodic quizzes, written assignments, viva voce, and mid-term and end-term examinations to evaluate student progress and understanding. Self-directed Learning: Students will be encouraged to engage in independent study through guided reading, online resources, and optional assignments to deepen their knowledge beyond the classroom. 6. Course No : BIO G532 Course Title : BIOSTATISTICS & BIOMODELING Instructor-in-Charge : SUSHMITA BASU Instructor : Shibasish Chowdhury 1. Course Description: Biostatistics and Biomodeling course has two components. Biostatistics part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t-test, ANOVA etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations. Biomodeling is designed to provide students the first-hand experience of modelling biomolecules to elucidate the relationships between sequence, structure and function. Specifically, different computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules will be discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The student would learn how to collect data suitable for statistical analyses, understand the general features of the data collected, making statistical inferences and likelihood of occurrence of an event using probability calculations and tests of significance. 3. Course Description: The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course, a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepreneurship ventures in Food Biotechnology will be discussed. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The aim of this course is providing the students with basic knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food-related sectors. These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry including advanced techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology. 3. Course Number : SW E101 Course Title : Social Conduct 1 Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Rajneesh Choubisa Prof. Sangeeta Sharma 1. Course description: Emotional & Social Intelligence, Relationships & Identity, Laws & Campus Policies and Practice, Inappropriate Behavior & Consent, Substance Abuse, Emotional Maturity & Communication, Recognizing Harm & Promoting Safety. 2. Scope and Objective: This is the first of a two-part course that is a General Institute Requirement, for all students in the first year of any program. It is intended to equip students with core emotional, social and legal literacy for a healthy campus life. This includes conversations around gender, sexuality, mental health, understanding of boundaries and consent, prevention of sexual misconduct, promoting responsible digital behavior and building awareness against substance abuse. 3. Course learning outcomes: At the end of this part of the course, the student will be able to CLO1.Recognize and apply core emotional and social skills for campus well-being, including stress management, empathy, and self-awareness. CLO2. Understand and navigate relationships with peers, faculty, and family, with sensitivity to gender identity, sexuality, and high achievement pressures. CLO3. Identify and challenge harmful social myths and stereotypes related to gender roles, masculinity, and interpersonal dynamics. CLO4. Establish and respect personal boundaries in social, academic, and digital contexts. CLO5. Demonstrate awareness of campus policies, legal protections (including POSH), and the consequences of sexual misconduct. CLO6. Understand reporting mechanisms and institutional responsibilities in promoting a safe and inclusive campus environment. CLO7. Engage with mental health literacy, recognize signs of emotional distress, and promote openness around mental well-being. CLO8. Reflect on individual responsibility in building a safe, respectful, and accountable student community. 4. Text books and references: No textbooks are needed for the course. 5. Course Format & Weekly Workflow - The course is fully online, with all content on a separate learning interface hosted on the Campus LMS - Moodle, and is asynchronous. - Content will be released weekly and typically takes 30–60 minutes to complete. - Each week, we’ll let you know what to focus on - whether it’s something to reflect on, apply in real life, or just be aware of. You don’t have to memorize anything. Just bring your honest attention, and we’ll guide you through it. - Each week’s material will have a one-week deadline, except during campus festival weeks, where deadlines will be set before the festival begins. - No content will be released one week before and during the mid-semester exams, and the course will end one week before the comprehensive exams. - The content must be accessed by logging in to the campus LMS (Moodle). - Each week ends with a quiz on the learning interface. A full score is required to proceed and multiple attempts are allowed. - Completing that quiz will unlock a corresponding Moodle quiz, which you must attempt to mark the week’s content as complete. - Your progress is automatically saved on Moodle, so you can pause and return to the material anytime. Closing the window/tab will not result in losing progress. - We encourage you to share your feedback! You can post your thoughts and questions on the discussion forum, or use the feedback forms provided at the end of each week’s content. Our instructor team will respond to queries. 6. Course Description: The course includes fundamentals and techniques of technical drawing and standard practices of the same so that design ideas can be adequately communicated and produced. Course No. : BITS F111 Course Title : Thermodynamics Instructor-in-Charge : Amit Jain Tutorial Instructors : Pradipta Chattopadhyay 1. Course Description Concepts and laws of thermodynamics; thermodynamic properties; applications to closed and open systems; entropy and entropy generation; availability. 2. Scope and Objective Thermodynamics deals with energy, matter, and the laws governing their interactions. • To learn usefulness of laws of thermodynamics in the design of processes, devices, and systems involving effective utilization of energy and matter. • To understand the fundamentals and concepts of the laws of thermodynamics as applied to control mass and control volume systems. • To apply the fundamentals and concepts of the laws of thermodynamics to control mass and control volume systems and analyze them. • To examine the performance of engineering devices in light of the laws of thermodynamics. 3. To define, understand, apply and analyze the concept of irreversibility and availability to thermodynamic systems and to evaluate second law efficiency of thermodynamics systems and devices. 4. Text book (TB): • Fundamentals of Thermodynamics, 10ed An Indian Adaptation, Authors Claus Borgnakke, Richard E. Course No. : BITS F214 Course Title : Science, Technology and Modernity Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Natasha Hazarika 1. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of how science and technology interact with societal structures, economic systems, and global governance. The course begins with an introduction to foundational perspectives on technological change and scientific knowledge systems, offering a basic orientation to how technologies are developed and adopted. It then moves to the examination of Intellectual Property Rights and Innovation, focusing on real-world issues such as patent disputes, corporate competition, and the strategic control of innovation. The third and final module explores Science, Technology, and Social Stratification, encouraging students to consider how power, inequality, and institutional interests influence technological priorities and outcomes. Overall, it critically assesses the societal responsibilities and consequences of scientific and technological work in contemporary settings. 2. Text Book: Sismondo, Sergio, An Introduction to Science and Technology Studies, UK: Wiley-Blackwell, 2010. Jacob, Margaret. 1997. Scientific Culture and the Making of the Industrial West. New York: Oxford University Press. Friedman, Thomas L. 1999. The Lexus and the Olive Tree. New York: Anchor Books. 3. Reference Material- Books/Papers: Book chapters, Journal papers, and newspaper reports will be shared as reading materials with the students. 4. Course Format: The course format will be interactive with regular class discussions and several group exercises and presentations. Students are expected to prepare in advance with the help of reading material provided and through self-initiative. _ Pilani Campus Instruction Division 5. Evaluation/Grading:

Course Description: Linear equations and matrices, Determinants, Basis of Rn , Eigen Value, Eigen Vector, Linear transformations on Rn . Linear Programming: Geometric Solutions, Simplex Method, Duality, Post optimal Analysis, Transportation and Assignment Problem. Nonlinear Programming (Unconstrained optimization). 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The course is made for Pharmacy students keeping in mind the importance of Linear Algebra and Linear programming problems and their possible applications in various fields of science and engineering. Linear algebra begins with vectors and matrices – two of the most important practical concepts in mathematics. Whereas Linear programming is a method to achieve the best outcome in a mathematical model whose requirements are represented by linear relationships. Linear programming can be applied to various fields of study. It is used in business and economics, but can also be utilized for some engineering problems. Industries that use linear programming models include transportation, energy, telecommunications, and manufacturing. 3. Course learning outcomes: CLO1. Apply the concepts of matrix algebra, systems of linear equations, vector spaces, linear transformations, and eigenvalues/eigenvectors to solve mathematical problems arising in science and engineering. CLO2. Formulate and solve linear programming problems using graphical and simplex-based methods, analyze duality and post-optimality, and apply optimization techniques to transportation and assignment problems. CLO3. Analyze and solve basic nonlinear optimization problems using appropriate numerical optimization techniques, and interpret the results in the context of engineering and pharmaceutical applications. 4. Room No. : 5102 1. Course Description: Environment, human population, and industrialization; natural resources and the impact of man-made activities on them; structure and function of ecosystem, population ecology, biodiversity and its conservation, environmental pollution, social issues and the environment, and environmental impact assessment. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be ignorant of the environmental issues. In lieu of the situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India. The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (flora- fauna) and abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic factors in the functioning of the environment, the impact of anthropogenic activities on the environment, different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio-political and economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested students can take the learnings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other electives/projects in these areas. 3. Scope & Objective of the Course: A data structure is a way to organize large amounts of data, their relationships, and the opera- tions that can be applied to them. This course focuses on applying data structures like stacks, queues, linked lists, heaps, trees, and graphs, along with algorithmic techniques such as brute- force, greedy, divide-and- conquer, and dynamic programming, to solve real-world problems, in- cluding shortest paths in maps, spell checking, and social network analysis. topics_text: Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division FIRST SEMESTER 2026-27 COURSE HANDOUT (Part II) Date: 01.08.2026 In addition to part I (the General Handout for all courses, appended to the Timetable), this section provides further specific details regarding the Course. COURSE NO. : BITS F314 COURSE TITLE : GAME THEORY & ITS APPLICATIONS INSTRUCTOR-IN-CHARGE : PROF. BALAKRUSHNA PADHI INSTRUCTOR : PROF. RAHUL ARORA 1. COURSE DESCRIPTION This course introduces the fundamental concepts and analytical tools of game theory for studying strategic interactions among rational decision-makers. It covers the construction and classification of games with complete and incomplete Information, strategic behavior, and solution concepts, including dominant strategy equilibrium, iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS), Nash equilibrium, mixed strategy equilibrium, and static and dynamic games with and without complete Information. It also includes extensive-form games, finite- and infinitely-repeated games, Bayesian games, and the integration of linear programming with game-theoretic analysis. Emphasis is placed on applications to economics and public policy, including social choice and voting theory, trade, environmental economics, industrial organization, auctions, negotiations, and other strategic decision-making problems. 2. SCOPE AND OBJECTIVE OF THE COURSE Game Theory is a tool and is a beautiful mix of mathematics, economics, and psychology. Game theory is a technique for analyzing strategic problems across diverse settings. The foundation of Game Theory was laid by John von Neumann, who proved the fundamental minimax theorem in 1928 and published a book (co-authored with Oskar Morgenstern), Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, in 1944. Game Theory became a buzzword and attained particular glamour, with the Nobel Prize going to John Nash for his contributions to the Field, which has found applications in almost every branch of knowledge. Broadly, Game Theory can be divided into cooperative and non-cooperative game theory. This course deals only with non-cooperative games. The main objective is to introduce students to Game Theory & Its applications to the real world as a tool for logical thinking in a strategic interaction setting. 3. COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES The course would aim to illustrate economic & other real-world concepts and to make students adept at approaching financial problems from a game-theoretic perspective. CLO1) Understand the Fundamentals of Game Theory, including game construction, analysis, and solutions. CLO2) Able to apply game theory tools to real-world contexts such as economic, political & environmental settings, trade negotiations, environmental agreements, cartels, oligopolistic competition, and in social choice contexts, among others. CLO3) Understand the collective decision-making mechanisms using game-theoretic tools. CLO4) Gain exposure to games with imperfect Information, including understanding the basic concepts of Bayesian games (types, beliefs, and strategies). CLO5) Develop problem-solving and strategic thinking skills. 4. TEXTBOOKS AND REFERENCE BOOKS 4.1 Textbooks 1. Osborne, Martin J. (2004): An Introduction to Game Theory, Oxford University Press, India. 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 4.2 Reference Books 1. Webster, Thomas J. (2009): Introduction to Game Theory in Business and Economics, Segment Books. 2. Gibbons, Robert (2019). Primer in Game Theory. Pearson. 3. Dutta, P. K. (1999). Strategies and games: theory and practice. MIT Press. 4. Fudenberg, Drew & Tirole, Jean (2005): Game Theory, MIT Press. 5. Osborne, Martin J. & Rubinstein, Ariel (1994): A Course in Game Theory, The MIT Press Cambridge. 6. Dixit, A. K., & Skeath, S. (2015). Games of strategy: Fourth international student edition. WW Norton & Company. 7. Dixit, A. K., & Nalebuff, B. (2008). The art of strategy: a game theorist's guide to success in business & life. WW Norton & Company. 5. Course Format & Weekly Workflow The course will be conducted using a blended, student-centered, and outcome-based approach, incorporating regular lectures (three per week to study core concepts and applications through the usage of Blackboard & multimedia tools such as PowerPoint slides and video clippings) and interactive discussions during lectures (to encourage discussion on real-life cases and to promote critical thinking). The students’ progress throughout the course will be evaluated through a continuous assessment approach in accordance with the institute’s academic regulations. The grading will be relative and in accordance with the BITS academic regulations. Course Description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data-driven modelling of serial-chain manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision making; and high-level robot control through large language models/vision language models (using camera sensors). Each module contains hands-on sessions and project-based learning to emphasize implementation of intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that primarily focus on analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles. Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high-level cognitive reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands-on experiments, students will investigate how intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial-chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI-based approaches for developing intelligent robotic systems. CO2 Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation. CO3 Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators. CO4 Develop AI-enabled robotic applications that integrate vision to generate high-level task commands for autonomous robotic manipulation. _ Pilani Campus ACADEMIC GRADUATE STUDIES AND RESEARCH DIVISION 3. Course No : BITS F416 Course Title : Introduction to Nano Science Instructor-in-Charge : Prof. Sarbani Ghosh (sarbani.ghosh@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Class Timings : M W 5 Th 10 Hour 1. Course Description: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties of nanomaterials, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field. 3. Course Learning Outcomes: After successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: 1 Pilani Campus ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION ◦ Explain the fundamental principles of nanoscience, including size-dependent properties and quantum effects at the nanoscale. ◦ Describe and compare common synthesis techniques used for nanomaterials. ◦ Analyze the structure–property–application relationships of nanomaterials in areas such as electronics, energy, catalysis, and biomedical systems. 4. Iafrate, " Handbook of Nanoscience, Engineering and Technology", CRC Press, ed 3 (March 12, 2012) ISBN-13: 978-1- 4398-6016-8. Course No : BITS F 429 Course Title : Nanotechnology for Renewable Energy and Environment Instructor-in-charge : Aditya Singh 1. Course Description: This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macro- and nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and carbon nanotube-based energy storage systems, and the application of nanomaterials for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation, nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the environment, and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit society across diverse fields. This course is designed to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and skills required for advanced academic research or industrial careers in nanotechnology, with particular emphasis on applications in renewable energy and environmental sustainability. The course is divided into 3 modules as decribed below. o Module 1: General introduction to principles of nanoscience and technology o Module 2: Nanotechnology applications in the renewable energy sector o Module 3: Nanotechnology applications in the environmental sector. The specific topics covered under each module are listed in the course plan (refer to section 6 of this handout). 3. Course learning outcomes o Introduce the importance and application of nanomaterials and the origin of their unique properties. o Summarize the fabrication methods, characterization techniques, and operating principles of solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and CNT-based energy storage systems. o Explain the merits and motivation in the renewable energy and environmental sectors. o Define toxic effect of nanomaterials on human and environment, relative remediation and precautions. 4. Course No : BITS F446 Course Title : Pattern Recognition Instructor-in-Charge : Raj Kumar Gupta Instructors : NA 1. Course Description: This is a first course on Pattern recognition. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and develops the theoretical background for the pattern recognition. It goes on to discuss the different aspects like the preprocessing of a digital image, segmentation, representation and description and finally the object recognition. During the course, a flavour of matlab programming will also be given. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: Over the past 30 years or so, pattern recognition and automation have evolved into a mature subject embracing many topics and applications: these range from automatic (robot) assembly to automatic vehicle guidance, from automatic interpretation of documents to verification of signatures, and from analysis of remotely sensed images to checking of fingerprints and human blood cells. Currently, pattern recognition and automatic visual inspection are undergoing very substantial growth, neces- sary improvement in quality, safety and cost effectiveness being the stimulating factors. The course introduces the students to the fundamentals of digital images and various processing techniques that are applied to them not only to improve their quality but also to recognize them. 3. Textbooks: TB1. Digital Image Processing, R. C. Gonzalez and R. E. Woods, 3rd and above, Pearson Education Asia, 2007. References: Ref1. Image Processing, analysis and machine vision, M. Sonka, V. Course No. : BITS F463 Course Title : Cryptography Instructor In Charge : Ankan Pal (ankan.pal@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Description: This course is an introduction to the basic theory and practice of cryptographic techniques used in information security. The course is intended to understand the mathematical concepts used for designing cryptosystems. The focus would be on the mathematical concepts from Number Theory and Abstract Algebra. We will delve into topics such as encryption (private-key and public-key), digital signatures, user authentication, key management, cryptographic hashing, Network security protocols, public-key infrastructure, digital rights management, and advancement in modern cryptology such as Identity Based Encryption, Steganography and Watermarking, Post-Quantum Cryptography, and Zero- Knowledge protocols. Prerequisites: The course is self-contained, however a basic understanding of probability theory, complexity theory, and modular arithmetic from number theory would be helpful. The course is intended for advanced undergraduates and master students. Course Objectives: Lectures deal with mathematical cryptography and related mathematical concepts required for modern cryptography and information security. The objective is to discuss and learn about basic tools and applications used in modern cryptography and to learn about some cryptographic protocols. On successful completion of the course students should be able to: understand basic principles and results of the theory of secure communication; know principles and problems of basic cryptosystems for encryption (both private and public key), digital signing and authentication; know methods to create core cryptographic protocols primitives; analyze and practically use simple cryptosystems; be understand basic principles of post-quantum cryptography and steganography. _ Pilani Campus Instruction Division Course Learning Outcomes. Utilize mathematical structures and ideas from Number Theory and Abstract Algebra to design and attack Cryptographic Protocols. CLO3. Construct and Analyse various symmetric-key and public-key Cryptosystems. CLO4. Reason and measure security of various Cryptosystems using computational and probabilistic techniques. CLO5. Design and Analyse common cryptanalytic attacks and tools. CLO6. Design secure communication mechanisms for the real-world using appropriate cryptographic primitives. CLO7. Implement and Evaluate cryptographic algorithms with respect to security and computational efficiency. CLO8. Course No. : ECON F415 & BITS F468 Course Title : New Venture Creation Instructor-In-Charge (Pilani & All Campuses) : Prof. Jyoti Tikoria + Dr. Paul Lopez Instructor-In-Charge (Hyderabad Campus) : Prof. Archana Srivastava Instructor-In-Charge (Goa Campus) : Prof. Himanshu Seth Instructor-In-Charge (Dubai Campus) : Prof. Vilas H Gaidhane Instructor-in-Charge (Ph.D. Drive Program) : Prof. Hitesh D Mathur Instructor-in-Charge (Design School) : Prof. Khushboo Jogani 1. Course Description: The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest- lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners? 3. Course Number : BITS F482/ECON F414 Course Title : Creating and Leading Entrepreneurial Organization Instructor-in-charge : JYOTI Team of Instructors : Prof. Arya Kumar 1. Course description: Fundamentals of Entrepreneurship; Elements of Leadership; Identifying Business Opportunities; Market Study and Research; Business Plans; Finance, Issues in Raising Finance, Venture Capitalist Evaluation of Business Plans, Technical Aspects for the Project; Corporate Strategies for Growth; Legal Aspects to entrepreneurship; People Skills; Marketing and Branding; Creativity and Communication. 2. Scope and Objective: This Course is about creating, managing, and leading an organization. This course helps in creating an entrepreneurial mindset, developing entrepreneurial skills and equipping students with the basic knowledge necessary for an entrepreneur. 3. Course learning outcomes: The course shall enable the participants to acquire and equip themselves with requisite knowledge and skills to start and run a business successfully, which is divided into personal skills (entrepreneurial skills) and those to start a company (Start-up tools). The learning outcomes are: a. To understand about entrepreneurship and getting inspiration from successful entrepreneurs. b. To learn about idea generation, opportunity assessment and evaluation and the process to create, build, and lead an entrepreneurial organization. c. To learn about nitty gritty of preparation of Business Plan. d. To know about different sources of funding and identify an appropriate source of funding for the venture. e. To learn about launching a business venture and growing it to next level of growth. 1 4. Barringer and R. Duane Ireland, Pearson Education, 2009. II. Entrepreneurship; Robert D Hisrich, Michael P Peters, and Dean A Shepherd, Tata McGraw Hill Publishing Company, New Delhi, 6 th ed., 2006. III. Patterns of Entrepreneurship, Jack M Kaplan, John Wiley & Sons, 2006. IV. Entrepreneurship New Venture Creation, David H Holt, Prentice Hall of India, New Delhi, 2004. V. The Handbook of Business enterprise, Kogan Page India Pvt. Ltd. 2003. VI. The Guru Guide o Entrepreneurship, Joseph H Boyett and Jimmie T Boyett, John Wiley & Sons, 2001. VII. Entrepreneurship Theory, Process, Practice, Donald F Kuratko and Richard M Hodgetts, Thomson Learning, 2007. 5. Method of conduct of the course: The approach used in this course focuses on learning by doing and learning by interactions. The effort of the instructor in this course is to be on the following:  Enable participants to understand the importance and relevance of entrepreneurship in the present era.  Motivating and inspiring them to take up entrepreneurship as a career option.  Enable them to understand the traits of an entrepreneur with a view to diagnose their own personality as to their strengths and weaknesses Vis-a- Vis ideal profile and to enable them to work out strategies to consciously inculcate desired skills.  Enabling participants to identify ideas, judge their potential as an entrepreneurial opportunity, select a particular opportunity within well-defined criteria, developing it further to concretize it to give it a shape of a business, with a focus on implementation strategies.  Develop skills to pitch their ideas for meeting their goals to raise finance.  Inculcate communication and negotiation abilities to manage situations and people.  Above all, to create an entrepreneurial environment that encourages participants to have zeal to learn by interaction and asking questions. Course description: Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA), dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO. 2. Course No. BITS U104 Course Title Foundations of Measurements and Experimentation Instructor-in-Charge Jayendra N. Bandyopadhyay Instructors Raj Kumar Gupta, Biswadip Shome, Sanjay Kumar Verma, Sushmita Basu, Soumya Saxena, Shraddha Gupta, Ajaya Kumar Pani, Bibhas R. Sarkar, Preeti Meena, Susmita Pradhan, Mukesh Kumar, Ravindra Dwivedi, Saurabh Gupta, M. Nyshitha Varma, Aneesh A. M., Hemant Sharma, A. R. Harikrishnan, Jagpreet Singh Sidhu, Aditi Pandey, Jyoti, Manjuladevi V., Jayendra N. Bandyopadhyay 1. Course Description: This course introduces scientific and engineering inquiry through the principles of measurement and experimentation. It covers fundamental concepts, such as accuracy, precision, calibration, error analysis, and uncertainty, as well as the hands-on use of sophisticated instruments across multiple disciplines. The course includes data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational tools. It emphasizes experimental design, hypothesis formulation, and experimental validation. It also focuses on correlating measurements with real-world problems, documenting and interpreting results, and communicating findings effectively with due consideration to ethical practices in experimentation. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: The course aims to provide a foundational understanding of measurement as an essential element of engineering and scientific practice. It covers key measurement concepts, exposure to a variety of instruments and sensors across disciplines, and methods for reliable data acquisition and analysis. The objectives of the course are to enable students to: (i) Understand fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, cali- bration, and uncertainty. (ii) Use appropriate measuring instruments and sensors for acquiring experimental data across dif- ferent domains. (iii) Apply techniques for data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational tools. (iv) Develop an understanding of experimental methodologies, including hypothesis formulation, experimental design, and validation. (v) Interpret experimental results and correlate them with underlying scientific and engineering principles. (vi) Communicate experimental findings effectively and adhere to ethical practices in experimen- tation and technical reporting. 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 3. Course Learning Outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: CO1: Understand and apply fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, calibration, and uncertainty. CO2: Use appropriate measuring instruments/sensors to solve a problem and acquire experimental data across different disciplines. CO3: Analyze experimental data using graphical and statistical methods, including error estimation and uncertainty propagation. CO4: Formulating hypotheses and their validation through design and conducting experiments. CO5: Interpret experimental observations using fundamental scientific and engineering principles. CO6: Document and communicate experimental findings effectively through structured reports and presentations. 4. Textbook: There is no textbook for this course. Lab manuals will be distributed to the students. 5. Reference Books: (i) Measurement Systems: Application and Design, Ernest O. Doebelin, McGraw-Hill, 2004, 5th Ed. (ii) Data Reduction and Error Analysis for the Physical Sciences, Philip R. Bevington and D. K. Robinson, McGraw-Hill, 2003, 3rd Ed. (iii) An Introduction to Error Analysis, John R Taylor, 2nd Ed, University Science Books, 1997. (iv) The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, Edward R. Tufte, Graphics Pr., 2001. 6. Course No. : CE F213 Course Title : SURVEYING Instructor In-Charge : Prof. Selva Balaji M (L & T1) Instructor : Thakur Ramjiram Singh (RS) (T2 & P1), Pratik Shashwat (RS) (P1 & P2), Meeniga Venkateswaralu (RS) (P1 & P2), Harish Kuppili (RS) (P2) Course Description: The compulsory disciplinary course has been designed to introduce the basic concepts of geodesy (surveying) for Civil Engineering students. Different basic and advanced methods of measurements and traversing have been included so that the student will be able to handle a given project independently, irrespective of whether it is a road or any other infrastructure project. Important issues like curve setting, calculation of areas and volumes, which form part and parcel of any field civil engineer in his/her day-to-day activity. Hence, in this course, these areas have also been included. Scope & Objective: The course introduces the students to various basic techniques in surveying, viz., chain, compass, theodolite, plane table, tacheometry, traversing, and calculation of areas and volumes, along with fundamentals of a few advanced surveying techniques. Course Learning Outcomes: After successful completion of this course, students will be able to: ▪ Understand and apply the fundamental concepts of surveying, including methods of linear measurements and handling common field equipment such as chains, tapes, and compasses. ▪ Execute and analyze compass traversing, including the computation and correction of bearings, and apply techniques for accurate plotting and area determination. ▪ Perform differential and profile levelling and interpret level books for reduced level determination, accounting for curvature and refraction. ▪ Conduct contouring operations and generate contour maps using field measurements and appropriate plotting techniques. 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division ▪ Carry out plane table and tacheometric surveys and apply relevant graphical and mathematical methods for plotting and distance/elevation computations. ▪ Design and set out simple and transition curves for civil infrastructure projects using chain, tape, and theodolite methods. ▪ Compute areas and volumes from cross-sections and contour maps and interpret mass haul diagrams relevant to earthworks. ▪ Demonstrate knowledge of modern surveying technologies, including total stations, photogrammetry, and remote sensing, and their practical applications. ▪ Analyze sources of error in surveying measurements and apply appropriate corrections to enhance the accuracy and reliability of data. ▪ Apply theoretical knowledge in field conditions by conducting various practical exercises such as chain surveying, curve setting, and use of total stations and GIS software. Scope and Objective: The course deals with properties, characterization, testing, selection and quality control of construction material. Course No : CE F231 Course Title : Fluid Mechanics Instructor-in-Charge : Dr. Guntu Ravikumar (M W 5 Th 10 at 6104) Tutorial Instructors : Dr. Guntu Ravikumar, Mr. Utkarsh Chaudhry, Ms. N Archana (F 1: T1, T2 at 6105) 1. Course Description: Fluid Mechanics is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics, especially the classical and well-established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following topics: Concepts and definitions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics, buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and similitude. The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: • Introduction to different fluid properties and their engineering applications • Learn about pressure exerted by fluids and pressure measurement techniques • Estimate hydrostatic forces on surfaces • Learn about buoyancy and evaluate stability of submerged and floating bodies • Understand concepts of fluid kinematics, methods of describing fluid flow, types of fluid flow, control mass and control volume, rate of flow, continuity equation, potential and stream functions • Study dynamics of fluid flow, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications, Navier Stokes equation, and pipe bend problems • Compute fluid discharge through orifices and mouthpieces, and flow over weirs and notches • Analyze flow of viscous fluids through pipes and plates, and compute head loss due to friction • Compute different types of energy losses and determine hydraulic gradient and total energy line for flow through pipes. Become adept at solving problems pertaining to syphon, flow through pipes in series, parallel and branched pipes, power transmission through pipes, and flow through nozzles • Perceive the concepts of dimensional analysis and similitude 3. Course Learning Outcomes: On completion of this course, the students will be able to, 1. Demonstrate the difference between solid and fluid, its properties and properties in static and dynamic conditions 2. Estimate pressure exerted by fluids and experiment with pressure measurement devices 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 3. Apply conservation laws applicable to fluids and its applications through fluid kinematics and dynamics 4. Perceive and formulate relationship among the parameters involved in the given fluid phenomenon and apply concepts of similitude in analyzing models and prototypes 5. Estimate the losses in pipelines for both laminar and turbulent conditions and analysis of pipes connected in series and parallel. 4. Course Description: This course introduces Civil Engineering students to the core concepts of hydraulic engineering, focusing on the Behaviour of real fluids: boundary layer theory, turbulent flow through conduits; analysis of closed-conduit hydraulic systems including pipes, valves, fittings, and pumps, water hammer in pipes, pipe networks analysis: Hardy cross method; Open channel hydraulics: uniform and non- uniform flow; flow past immersed bodies: drag and lift; Analysis of Impact of jets; Introduction to fluid machinery. 2. Scope & Course Objective: The problems encountered by our society, such as water supply, irrigation, navigation, and water power, resulted in the development of Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulic Engineering. The objective of this course is to equip students with a fundamental understanding of the principles of fluid mechanics as applied to hydraulic systems and structures. The course aims to achieve the following Course Objectives (Teacher's perspective), aligned with the Course Outcomes (COs) (Students’ perspective): 1. To develop an analytical understanding of flow behavior in pipes and channels under varying conditions. 2. To apply fluid mechanics principles in analyzing hydraulic systems, including energy losses and force impacts. 3. To introduce the working principles and performance of fluid machinery relevant to civil engineering. 4. To prepare students for practical problem-solving in the analysis, design, and assessment of water infrastructures of Pipe networks, open channels, and structures submerged in fluid, like bridge piers, dealt with by civil engineers. 3. Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs): Upon the completion of this course, students will be able to perform the following: 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division CLO1. Explain the behaviour of real fluids, including boundary layer development and turbulent flow through conduits, and apply these concepts to practical hydraulic engineering problems. CLO2. Analyze closed-conduit hydraulic systems by evaluating head losses, pipe flow characteristics, pumps, valves, fittings, and the effects of water hammer in pressurized pipelines. CLO3. Analyze and solve pipe network problems using the Hardy Cross Method for the design and operation of water distribution systems. CLO4. Analyze uniform and non-uniform flow in open channels using fundamental hydraulic principles and empirical equations for engineering design and performance assessment. CLO5. Evaluate fluid forces on immersed bodies, including drag, lift, and the impact of jets on stationary and moving surfaces, for engineering applications. CLO6. Explain the classification, operating principles, and applications of fluid machinery, particularly hydraulic turbines and pumps, and relate them to hydraulic engineering systems. 4. Course Description: Design Philosophies: Introduction to working stress design philosophy; Limit State design philosophy, Limit State design of Singly reinforced and doubly reinforced rectangular and flanged section beams; Design of one-way and two-way slabs in flexure; Design of beams and slabs for shear; Design of beams and slabs for bond, anchorage and development length; Design of beams and slabs for serviceability; Limit state design of columns subjected to axial load, and axial load plus uni-axial and bi-axial bending; Design of footings under the columns; Design of simple staircases. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course In this course, the students will be introduced to the various design philosophies used in the design of Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures, with a particular focus on the Limit State Design method. The course will provide an in-depth discussion of the concepts of Limit State Design method. Subsequently, the Limit State Design method will be employed to the design of singly and doubly reinforced rectangular- and T-section beams and one-way and two-way slabs, for flexure, shear, anchorage, bond, and serviceability requirement. Additionally, the course will cover the design of columns subjected to axial loads, and axial load plus uniaxial and biaxial moments. Moreover, the course will explore different types of staircases, with a specific emphasis on the design of dog-legged staircases. At the end of this course, students will be able to design the basic structural elements of an RC buildings. 3. Text Book and References TB: S. Course Number: CE F331 Course Title: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering Instructor-in-charge: Dr. Sayantan Chakraborty Course description: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering is an introductory course to various in-situ test methods pertaining to geotechnical engineering and analysis of in-situ test results, including drilling and sampling, standard penetration test (SPT), cone-penetration test (CPT), piezocone penetration test (CPTu), vane shear test (VST), non-destructive tests (NDT) using body waves and surface waves - seismic reflection test, seismic refraction test, and spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) test. Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs will be discussed. The contents of this course will enable students to utilize different in-situ test results for soil property interpretation, direct and indirect applications for the design of geotechnical structures, and liquefaction assessment. Course Number : CE G515 Course Title : Fundamentals of Systems Engineering Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Rallapalli Srinivas [Team of Instructors] : Prof. Rallapalli Srinivas Timings : T Th F (3rd: 10 am to 11 am), 1226 1. Course description: Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems across their entire life cycle—from conceptual design and planning to operation, maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical, organizational, and stakeholder-related complexities by employing a holistic, systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments. 2. Scope and Objective: The course is designed to build a strong foundation in systems engineering methodologies while contextualizing their application to infrastructure planning, development, and management. Students will explore systems architecture, modeling, simulation, optimization, and decision-support frameworks relevant to the life cycle of infrastructure systems. The course also integrates modern tools such as AI, IoT, digital twins, and life-cycle costing techniques to support informed decision-making and innovation. The overarching objective is to develop technically sound, system-aware professionals capable of solving real-world infrastructure problems through interdisciplinary thinking, structured analysis, and evidence-based planning. 3. Course learning outcomes: a. Understand systems engineering principles and their application to infrastructure life-cycle management. b. Apply systems thinking and modeling techniques to analyze complex infrastructure systems. c. Use optimization, simulation, and decision-support tools for infrastructure planning and operations. d. Evaluate infrastructure projects using life-cycle costing and basic investment analysis methods. e. Introduction to Integrating emerging technologies such as AI and IoT into infrastructure systems design and management. 4. Text books and references: TB1. Blanchard, B. S., & Fabrycky, W. J. (2010). Course No. : CE G525 Course Title : Water Resources Planning and Management Instructor-in-charge : AJIT PRATAP SINGH Website of I/C : https://www.bits-pilani.ac.in/pilani/ajit-pratap-singh/ https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ajit-Pratap-Singh 1. CE G525 Course Description Introduction; Quantitative and qualitative assessment of water resources; Engineering principles applied to the management of water resources; Hydrographic and project surveys; Watershed management; Measurement techniques in water resources engineering; Gains of water resources planning to the society; Water economics; Computer utilization areas; Project discussions; Laboratory experiments. 2. Scope & Objective The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning and management of water resources. It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water systems, integrating surface and groundwater hydrology, water quality modeling, and watershed management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems. The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible water resource development and policy-making. 3. Course learning outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: a. Understand the structure, components, and modeling approaches of water resource systems. b. Apply principles of engineering and economics in water resource planning and project evaluation. c. Analyze point and non-point source pollution using water quality modeling techniques. d. Assess groundwater resources and apply methods for sustainable groundwater management. e. Perform statistical and uncertainty analyses related to streamflow and water availability. f. Formulate and solve water resource problems using linear, non-linear, and multi-objective optimization techniques. g. Plan and manage reservoir operations under both deterministic and stochastic environments. h. Utilize modern tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence in water resource management. i. Evaluate real-world case studies and apply integrated approaches to address complex water management challenges. Text Books: T1. Vedula S. and P. P. Course description: [as per the Bulletin] This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including soil, aggregates, bitumen,bituminous mixtures and pavement quality concrete (PQC). Soil characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties, classification, compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade soil. For aggregates, origin and production, mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed. Detailed description of bituminous binder would include origin, production and it application, chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties, mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would be covered along with design example. 2. A brief about the ongoing worldwide research on various material aspects of pavements will also be covered as a part of different lectures. 3. Course learning outcomes: a. . Course Number : CE G551 Course Title : DYNAMICS OF STRUCTURES Instructor-in-charge : DIPENDU BHUNIA [Team of Instructors] : NONE 1. Course description: Introduction and Scope of dynamic analysis of structures; origins of vibration theory and experiment; review of earlier concepts: D’Alembert’s principle, equations of motion. Elements of a structural system: springs, dashpot, mass; Springs in parallel and series; methods to formulate equations of motion; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped free vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped forced vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Forced vibration under harmonic, periodic, impulse, step, ramp, general dynamic forces (time and frequency domain analysis) and response spectrum load, support excited vibration, seismic pickups; Numerical techniques for evaluation of dynamic response of SDOF system; time domain analysis; direct integration techniques; finite difference method (Central Difference method); Newmark beta method; average and linear acceleration method; Development of equation of motion and solution for two degree of freedom systems; Free vibration analysis of MDOF systems; frequencies; mode shapes and response; orthogonality condition of mode shapes; Approximate methods for obtaining natural frequencies and mode shapes; Holzer method; Stodola’s method; Rayleigh’s method; Rayleigh-Ritz method; Inverse iteration method; Vector iteration method; Rayleigh’s Quotient iteration method; Matrix iteration method; Generation of damping matrix for MDOF; dynamic properties; modal damping; classical damping; damped response with Rayleigh and Caughey damping.Mode superposition method; mode acceleration method; modal combination rules using absolute sum, SRSS and CQC method. 2. Scope and Objective: Natural phenomena and human activities impose forces of time-dependent variability on various civil engineering structures. This course deals with analysis and design of structures subjected to dynamic loads, which involve consideration of time-dependent forces. Based on this scope, the following objectives have been listed:  To make this course necessary for students who are desirous of joining design offices/ industry related to buildings, industrial plants, bridges, tanks, offshore structure, tall chimneys etc.  To determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced vibration force etc. 3. Course learning outcomes: a. Development of software for the analysis of framed/skeleton structures. b. Capability development for the use of structural dynamics concept and its applications for framed structural analysis and design under dynamic loading. c. Determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure, which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced vibration force etc. 4. Text books and references: TB1. Anil K. Chopra, “Dynamics of Structures: Theory and applications to earthquake engineering”, Prentice Hall India Ltd., 2007. TB2. Mukhopadhyay,M., “Structural Dynamics: Vibrations & Systems” Ane Books Pvt. Ltd., 2006. RB1. R.W. Clough and J. Penzien, “Dynamics of Structures”, McGraw Hill International edition, 1993. RB2. Paz,M., “Structural Dynamics: Theory & Computation” CBS Publishers & Distributors, 2001. 5. [Method of conduct of the course] The course will be conducted primarily through Chalkboard with ppt as well online medias such as Google class and/or Nalanda. Course No : CE G613 Course Title : ADVANCED CONCRETE STRUCTURES Instructor-in-Charge : G MUTHUKUMAR 1. Course Description: The course deals with various aspects of concrete structures with emphasis on design of various elements and exposure to different code provisions. Materials; high strength concrete, flexure analysis and design; shear and diagonal tension; bond and anchorage; serviceability; torsion; columns; joints; indeterminate beams and frames; yield line analysis; strip method for slabs; composite construction; footing and foundations; concrete building system; concrete tall buildings, detailing in concrete structures 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The concrete structures are quite common in India for both low-rise and high-rise buildings due to the strong performance in the last many decades even during strong wind & earthquake ground motion. The concrete structures are used in most of the infrastructure applications such as construction of buildings, bridges, roads, airport structures, stadiums, water tanks, chimneys, storage bins, nuclear reactors etc., The codal provisions are continuously changing with changing times due to technological advancements and our improved understanding of the behavioral characteristics of concrete. Though concrete structures are design are not anything new, but certain aspects of design and construction still needs further research and understanding. The beam-column joint is hardly 50 years old and was totally unexplored before 1970s. Today, it was observed that beam-column failure is one of the most important reasons for the failure of RC framed structures. On the other hand, RC structures are only framed form, but different structural configurations evolve over the years to accommodate the tall buildings with safety and economy. The present course aims to highlight the design and construction aspects of wide range of structures, ranging from traditional RC framed structures to tall buildings to certain specialized structures such as chimneys and water tanks. The emphasis will be more on the performance of structure under earthquake loading conditions. The codal provisions will be discussed for the better understanding. ➢ To understand the concrete structures and its applications [Module - I] ➢ To study different structural configurations for the concrete structures [Module-II] ➢ To understand and design few important components of RC framed structures including beam-column joints and other vital structural elements [Module-III] ➢ To understand the concept of shear wall frame structures [Module IV] ➢ To understand the behavioral and design aspects of shell structures and folded plates [Module V] ➢ To understand the ductile behavioral aspects of structures under earthquake [Module VI] ➢ To understand the design and detailing aspects of water tanks and chimneys [Module VII] ➢ To understand the design aspects of RCC poles and pipes [Module VIII] 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division ➢ To discuss the case studies of different RC structures and its failures [Module IX] ➢ To discuss the various advancements in concrete structures and the research scope [Module X] 3. Course No. : CE G614 Course Title : PRESTRESSED CONCRETE STRUCTURES Instructor In-charge : Prof. Subhasis Pradhan 1. Course Description Introduction to basic concepts of prestressing; prestressing systems; analysis of prestress; losses in prestress; deflection; design of anchorage zone, design of prestressed concrete girders. 2. Scope and Objectives The universal use of prestressed concrete as a versatile construction material is well established due to its suitability in multifarious types of structural applications. The application of prestressed concrete is increasing with the development of technology. Prestressing is the application of an initial load on a structure to enable it to counteract the stresses arising from subsequent loads during its service period. In this course, the students will be introduced to prestressed concrete and its applications. The course would cover important topics of prestressed concrete, including the design of structural elements based on the limit state philosophy of design. It would partially fulfill the requirements of practicing structural design engineers. The course integrates science and engineering principles to design prestressed concrete members and structural systems. The application of scientific and engineering knowledge would be demonstrated in solving engineering problems associated with the design of precast prestressed building members. This course would be quite helpful for students who want to join the structural design or construction industry. At the end of the coursework, students will be able to determine the behavior of prestressed concrete structures. 2. Course Learning Outcomes Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to understand the fundamental concepts of prestressing and the different systems used in prestressed concrete construction. They will gain the ability to – ▪ Understand the basic principles of prestressing and identify various prestressing systems including pre-tensioning and post-tensioning methods. 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division ▪ Analyze the behaviour of prestressed concrete members under axial loads and bending, including the use of pressure/thrust lines and load balancing concepts. ▪ Calculate different types of prestress losses and understand their causes and effects on structural performance. ▪ Evaluate the flexural and shear strength of prestressed concrete members and design appropriate reinforcements. ▪ Analyze the transfer of prestress in pre-tensioned members and anchorage zone stresses in post- tensioned members. ▪ Design prestressed concrete sections for flexure using limit state concepts and apply methods such as Magnel’s approach. ▪ Compute short- and long-term deflections in prestressed concrete members and assess crack width control under service loads. ▪ Analyze statically indeterminate prestressed concrete structures, including secondary moments and concordant cable profiles. ▪ Understand and design composite structures involving prestressed and in-situ cast concrete under different support conditions. ▪ Apply engineering knowledge and analytical skills to solve real-world structural design problems involving prestressed concrete. 3. Scope and Objective of the Course: Bridges are an inseparable part of any communication network as they are the key elements in roadways and highway networks. This course intends to impart skills for analysis & design of various types of bridges.
