COURSE NUMBER : ECON F213 COURSE TITLE : MATHEMATICAL AND STATISTICAL METHODS INSTRUCTOR-IN-CHARGE : PROF. RAHUL ARORA Email: rahul.arora@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in Chamber Number: 6165 D 1. COURSE DESCRIPTION The course is designed to provide a basic understanding of various statistical and mathematical methods useful for decision-making and for understanding applications in other economics and finance courses. The course is divided into two parts: Statistical Methods and Mathematical Methods. Statistical Methods include methods of collecting and describing statistical data – types of data and data collection methodologies, sampling methods & design, data describing methods (graphical and numerical); Correlation and Regression analyses; Index numbers: Concepts, uses, and methods of construction; Analysis of Time-series: Components, data generating process, and stationarity; Statistical Inference: Introduction to Probability and its distributions, sampling distributions, theory of estimation, Tests of Hypotheses testing (Parametric & Non-Parametric); and Mathematical Methods include Concepts from Linear Algebra & their Applications (Matrices, Input-Output analysis, and Game Theory); Concepts from Calculus and their applications; Introduction to Optimization in Economics and its Applications. 2. SCOPE AND OBJECTIVE The main objective is to learn how to use mathematical and statistical methods in economics. It involves a review of the fundamentals of mathematics and statistics, which can be used in applied economics. Knowledge of these fundamentals and their application in applied economics would help students better understand the entire economic system and the policymaking process. At the end of this course, students will be able to understand and solve graduate-level problems in economics and finance using the knowledge they have gained. Specifically, this course uses fundamentals from calculus, algebra, optimization, and basic statistics. This course would lay the foundation for students to understand related courses in economics and finance, such as econometrics and growth theory. 3. COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES CLO1. Apply appropriate methods for data collection, sampling, organization, and descriptive analysis, using graphical and numerical techniques to summarize and interpret statistical data. CLO2. Analyze relationships among economic and business variables using correlation and regression techniques, and construct and interpret index numbers for relevant applications. CLO3. Analyze time-series data by identifying its components, understanding the underlying data-generating process, and assessing stationarity. CLO4. Apply probability concepts and statistical inference techniques, including probability and sampling distributions, estimation, and parametric and non-parametric hypothesis testing, to draw valid conclusions from data. CLO5. Apply mathematical methods to economic problems, using concepts from linear algebra, input-output analysis, game theory, calculus, and optimization to formulate and solve economic decision problems. 4. TEXTBOOKS AND REFERENCE BOOKS 4.1 Textbook TB1S - Statistics – Lind, Douglas A., Marchal, William G., and Wathen, Samuel A., Statistical Techniques in Business and Economics, McGraw-Hill, 14th International Edition (2010). TB1M - Mathematics – Alpha. C. Chiang, Fundamental Methods of Mathematical Economics, 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division McGraw-Hill, 3rd Edition. 4.2 Reference Books • RB1.– David R. Anderson, Dennis J. Sweeney, and Thomas A. Williams, Statistics for business and economics, 9th Edition (2005). • RB2. – Ken. Black, Business Statistics for Contemporary Decision Making, Wiley India, 4th Edition (2004). • RB3. – S.P. Gupta, Statistical Methods, Sultan Chand and Sons, 43rd Edition (2014). • RB4. – Knut Sydsaeter, and Peter T. Hammond, Mathematics for Economic Analysis, Pearson Education, 1st Edition (reprint 2002). • RB5: Webster, Thomas J. (2009): Introduction to Game Theory in Business and Economics, Segment Books. 5. Course Format & Weekly Workflow The course will be conducted using a blended, student-centered, and outcome-based approach, incorporating regular lectures (three per week to study core concepts through usage of blackboard & multimedia tools such as PowerPoint slides, video clippings), tutorial classes (one per week for problem solving and explaining numerical exercises through blackboard/slides/statistical software), and interactive discussions during lectures (to encourage discussion on real-life cases and to promote critical thinking). The students’ progress throughout the course will be evaluated through continuous assessment in accordance with the institute’s academic regulations. The grading will be relative and in accordance with BITS academic regulations. The course will use NALANDA, a learning management system (LMS), to display course information, including lecture slides/notes, tutorial sheets, solution material, and other related materials. Course Number : ECON F214 Course Title : ECONOMIC ENVIRONMENT OF BUSINESS Instructor-in-Charge : PROF. SURUCHI SHRIMALI Tutorial/Practical Instructor : Prof. Suruchi Shrimali 1. Course Description: Businesses are the driving force behind a nation's economic activity since they enable its population to attain a higher quality of living. It is essential to understand that a business firm does not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions, and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting its performance. Business enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So, the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with its environment would generally determine its success or failure. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The course aims to (1) Create familiarity with economic environment concepts and indicators, economic policies, and economic regulation (2) Develop the ability to analyze and anticipate changes in the economic environment and, (3) Enable students to take more effective business decisions by being responsive to the changing external economic environment. The objective of this course is to unravel all those economic factors that are external to and beyond the control of individual business enterprises and their management, with a focus on the Indian context. 3. Learning Outcome of the Course: This course will educate students on the interdependencies and linkages between business and its environment, focusing on the Indian context. Moreover, it will improve comprehension of various external economic factors affecting the business environment. For instance, the business climate in India is influenced by variables such as GDP, inflation, fiscal policy, monetary policy, industrial policy, etc., which have both direct and indirect effects. Furthermore, it will thoroughly comprehend many economic elements in the business environment more pragmatically. 4. Textbooks and Reference Books 4.1 Text Books (TB): TB1. The students’ progress throughout the course will be evaluated through a continuous assessment approach as per the institute’s academic regulations. Course No. : ECON F311 Course Title : INTERNATIONAL ECONOMICS Instructor-in-charge : Prof. GEETILAXMI MOHAPATRA Tutorial Instructor : Prof. Geetilaxmi Mohapatra 1. Course Description This course develops a systematic exposition of both classical and modern theories of international trade in goods and services that try to explain the composition, direction, and consequences of international trade, and the determinants and effects of trade policy. The course will look critically at the welfare and profit implications of trade policy deviations from free trade. It then builds on the models of open economy macroeconomics. 2. Scope and objective of the course:  To understand the effects of international trade on individuals and businesses  To understand the effects of changes in trade policies on trade  To apply macroeconomic models to understand the international economy.  To focus on the interrelationships among aggregate economic variables such as GDP, unemployment rates, inflation rates, trade balances, exchange rates, interest rates, etc.  To focus on the significance of trade imbalances, the determinants of exchange rates, and the aggregate effects of government monetary and fiscal policies. 3. Course No. : ECON F313 Course Title : ISSUES IN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT Instructor-In-Charge : Prof. BALAKRUSHNA PADHI Instructor : Prof. Balakrushna Padhi Tutorial/Practical Instructors : Prof. Balakrushna Padhi 1. Course Description: This course provides a comprehensive and contemporary examination of the major issues, challenges, and policy debates in economic development by integrating theoretical perspectives, empirical evidence, and real-world applications. It views development as a multidimensional process that extends beyond economic growth to encompass structural transformation, human development, institutional quality, technological progress, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. The course explores why countries experience divergent development trajectories and examines the roles of markets, governments, institutions, globalization, and technological change in shaping long- run development outcomes. Drawing upon classical and contemporary development theories, with particular emphasis on India and other developing economies, the course examines a broad range of development issues, including poverty, inequality, unemployment, population dynamics, demographic transition, migration, urbanization, education, health, agriculture, industrialization, infrastructure, financial inclusion, foreign investment, governance, environmental degradation, climate change, artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Through analytical frameworks, empirical evidence, policy debates, and case studies, students will develop the ability to critically examine development challenges, interpret development indicators, and evaluate alternative policy interventions for achieving sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development. 2. Scope and Objective: The primary objective of this course is to equip students with a rigorous understanding of the theoretical, empirical, and policy dimensions of economic development while fostering the analytical skills required to evaluate contemporary development challenges. The course enables students to understand the economic, social, institutional, technological, and environmental factors that influence development outcomes across countries and regions. It emphasizes the interrelationships among economic growth, structural transformation, employment generation, poverty reduction, income distribution, human capital formation, institutional development, and environmental sustainability. Students will critically examine competing development theories and policy paradigms, evaluate the effectiveness of development strategies adopted by different countries, and analyze the role of public policy in promoting inclusive and sustainable development. The course also introduces emerging issues that are reshaping development discourse, including artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, climate resilience, financial inclusion, gender equality, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Equal emphasis is placed on developing students' analytical, quantitative, and research competencies through the interpretation of development indicators, evaluation of empirical evidence, policy analysis, and application of contemporary development concepts to real- world economic issues. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess development policies and contribute to evidence-based decision-making in both academic and policy contexts. 1 ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION 3. Course learning outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO1. Explain and critically evaluate the major theories, concepts, and contemporary issues in development economics, including economic growth, structural transformation, poverty, inequality, employment, human development, institutional change, globalization, environmental sustainability, and emerging issues such as artificial intelligence and digital transformation. CLO2. Apply appropriate analytical, quantitative, and empirical tools to interpret development indicators, assess the effectiveness of development policies and programmes, and evaluate alternative strategies for promoting sustainable, inclusive, and equitable economic development at national and international levels. CLO3. Critically analyze contemporary development challenges using theoretical and empirical evidence, formulate evidence-based policy recommendations, and undertake independent research on key issues affecting developing economies, with particular reference to India and other emerging economies. 4.1 Textbook: 1. Course No : ECON F 315 / FIN F 315 Course Title : Financial Management Instructor-in-Charge : Rajan Pandey 1. Course Description: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies. 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2. The structure of the course enables students to: a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations, b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities, statistics, and MS-Excel. 3. Course No. ECON F354 / FIN F311 Course Title Derivatives & Risk Management Instructor (s) Prof. Aditya Sharma Instructor-in-charge Prof. Aditya Sharma 1. Scope & Objective: The objective of this course is to provide students an introductory level familiarity with a particular type of financial instruments known as DERIVATIVES. To achieve the stated objectives, the course provides a detailed description on the structure (read, design) and utility (read, relevance) of the most common and popular financial derivatives namely, Options, Futures, and Swaps. The scope of the course entails acquainting students with the mechanics of trading and settlement of derivative instruments in the financial markets and their function as insurance products for hedging financial risk. No understanding about financial instruments or their derivatives is complete without a thorough grasp over interest rate concepts and hence the course also includes discussion on topics such as time value of money, term structure of interest rates and their role in valuation of bonds, computation of yield and forward interest rates, estimating bond-price volatility, and the role of bond duration and convexity in mitigating interest rate risks. The topics covered in the course will, at an introductory level, enable participants to learn about common risks prevalent in the financial markets and how to manage its impact on investment exposure by using derivatives. Discussion on valuation of financial derivatives and a brief introduction to creating synthetic investment positions by combining derivatives prepares students for advanced level courses such as Financial Engineering and Financial Risk Analytics and Management. The course concludes with a survey of selective topics of contemporary interest to risk management industry such as forecasting volatility, estimating value-at-risk, etc. The topics covered in the course will also assist students in preparing for competitive professional international certifications such as Financial Risk Manager (FRM) and Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA). 2. Prerequisites: This is an elementary course on Derivatives and Risk Management and does not assume any prior knowledge of Financial Markets, Instruments and Derivatives. However, familiarity of basic economic theory such as law of supply and demand, utility maximization principle, compounding and discounting of cash flows, etc. are desirable. The course is not mathematically rigorous and a first-year course on elementary linear algebra, calculus, probability, and differential equations will be sufficient to grasp the contents of the course. It is expected that students have technical know-how of MS excel as it will be used to demonstrate required computations, wherever required, and for carrying out take-home assignments. Course No. : ECON F355 Course Title : BUSINESS ANALYSIS AND VALUATION Instructor-In-Charge : Dr. Aprajita Pandey 1. Course Description: This course focuses on the essential tools and frameworks for evaluating the value of companies through financial analysis. Students will explore key concepts such as internal growth, mergers and acquisitions, along with valuation methodologies like discounted cash flow and relative valuation. Designed for those with prior knowledge in finance and accounting, the course equips students with the skills to analyze financial statements, assess market conditions, and identify key performance drivers. Ideal for aspiring professionals in investment banking, corporate finance, and consulting, this course enhances analytical capabilities and strategic thinking in business valuation and decision-making. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The Process of measuring and managing the value of companies is a central aspect of financial analysis. Globally, managers are in pursuit of adding value to their firms via two important means. One, by enhancing the firm’s productive capacity through internal (or organic) growth, which has a simultaneous positive impact on its stock price. Second, through mergers and acquisitions (a decision involving factors external to the firm) that interlocks with corporation’s key strengths, and yield benefits in the long run. Hence, asking, “What is something worth?” is a vital question to business decision making, and the principal objective behind this course is to provide the learners with the conceptual basis, intuitive reasoning, and analytical framework to answer this question. The focus of this course is on valuing equity (or ownership) in a firm and estimating the value of the overall enterprise. The coverage relies on discounted cash flow, relative valuation, and contingent valuation approaches for extracting the value of a business. Since financial statements serve as the basis for all types of valuation methods, the course begins by providing brief framework on the principles governing the financial statements, and adjustments that are often required to capture the underlying business reality. Students who are either currently pursuing or would like to embark on a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting will find the course material to be most useful. The course also carries a broader appeal to individuals who are interested in enhancing their understanding of financial analysis, and in learning how businesses measure and create value for their investors. 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Important: This is not a beginning level course. The course presumes that you have a prior exposure on a variety of introductory concepts in finance, accounting, and statistics. For beginners, it is therefore highly recommended that they go through the introductory material in finance and accounting concepts at the earliest. Feel free to contact the I/C ASAP in case you are facing difficulty in following the classroom discussions. 3. Expected Learning Outcome of the Course: The course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of financial analysis, advanced accounting practices, and valuation techniques. By the end of the program, learners will be able to effectively analyze financial statements, gaining insights into an organization's performance and financial health. A critical component of the curriculum focuses on valuation methods, where students will learn to assess the value of assets and investments using various approaches, such as discounted cash flow analysis and market comparables. This knowledge will empower them to evaluate investment opportunities critically and make informed decisions that can significantly impact an organization's financial strategy. Overall, these outcomes will prepare students for successful careers in finance and accounting, equipping them with both analytical and practical skills essential for navigating complex financial landscapes. 4. Course Number : ECON F 412 / FIN F 313 Course Title : Security Analysis and Portfolio Management Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Arya Kumar Instructor : Prof. Rajan Pandey 1. Course description: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance. 2. Scope and Objective: The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to: • Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics. • Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance management. • Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation. • Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques. • Technical analysis. • Financial derivative contracts and their applications. 3. Course learning outcomes: • Distinguish the major classes of financial securities — equity, fixed income, derivatives and alternatives — by their claim structure, risk-return profile and role within a portfolio. • Value individual securities using techniques appropriate to the instrument, including discounted cash flow and relative valuation for equity and yield-based measures for fixed income, and state the assumptions on which each valuation rests. • Measure and decompose investment risk, separating systematic from unsystematic components, and evaluate investments on a risk-adjusted basis rather than on raw return. • Construct a diversified portfolio using correlation and modern portfolio theory, and justify the resulting asset allocation against a specified investor's objectives, time horizon and risk tolerance. • Apply derivative instruments to hedge or modify portfolio exposure, and explain the payoff profile and risk of each strategy employed. • Assess portfolio performance using risk-adjusted measures and attribution analysis, and determine when a portfolio requires rebalancing as market conditions change. 4. Course No : ECON F417/FIN F413 Course Title : RISK MANAGEMENT AND INSURANCE Instructor-in-Charge : N V M RAO Instructor(s) : -- Tutorial/Practical Instructors : -- 1 Course Description: Introduction to risk; types of risk; risk measurement; risk management techniques; risk avoidance, loss control, loss financing, risk retention, risk transfer, internal risk reduction through diversification etc.; insurance business and operations; insurance pricing; insurance v/s hedging; life, health and income risk; property and liability risk – commercial and personal; social insurance; insurance regulation 2 Scope and Objective of the Course: This course will examine the way in which business and society make an assessment of, control and transfer risk. The scope of this course is to provide a broad understanding of risk and insurance as a means to manage it. This forms the foundation to facilitate the students in their further studies on insurance. The course introduces the concept of risk and techniques of identifying, measuring and managing it. In this context, insurance as a risk management tool is discussed with references to its role, functions and basic principles as applicable to different classes of insurance. The objectives of the course are to provide students with  a comprehensive understanding for making risk management decisions to increase business value and individual welfare  a complete understanding of risk transfer through pooling and key features of insurance market  an understanding of the effects of and rationale for public policies that affect risk and its allocation  Knowledge about insurance markets and important details of an insurance contract as a risk management tool.  Assessing and evaluating insurance needs and implement effective solutions, involving and aligning the entire organization 3 Text Book: George Rejda and Michael McNamara ‘Principles of Risk Management and Insurance’ 14th edition, Pearson Education, 2022 (ISBN 9780134082578) 4 Reference Books:  John Teale, Insurance and Risk Management, CCH Australia Ltd, 2013  James Trieschmann, David Sommer, Robert Hoyt, Risk management and Insurance, Cengage Learning, 12 Edition, 2005  Harrington scott E.& Niehaus Gregory “Risk Management and Insurance” Tata McGraw-Hill, Second edition.2004 (or latest edition)  Scott E. Course Number : EE G508 Course Title : Urban Water Management Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Rallapalli Srinivas [Team of Instructors] : Prof. Rallapalli Srinivas Timings : M W (4rd: 11 am to 12 pm), T 10 (5 pm to 6 pm), 1233 1. Course description: Urban Water Management is an advanced course focusing on the planning, design, operation, and assessment of urban water systems under increasing pressures of population growth, urbanization, and climate change. It explores the complete urban water cycle, including supply, sanitation, drainage, and environmental flows, with strong emphasis on sustainable and resilient urban development. The course addresses technical, social, economic, and regulatory challenges through a multidisciplinary lens. Students are exposed to contemporary topics such as stormwater management, water-sensitive urban design, and water quality monitoring. Practical software-based training modules on stormwater modelling, flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics are integrated to bridge theory and real-world applications. Students will also gain insights into advanced asset management systems, sustainability indicators, GIS tools, and the effect of urbanization on hydrological behavior. This industry-oriented course prepares students for professional roles in government, consulting, and research sectors concerned with smart, equitable, and sustainable urban water solutions. 2. Scope and Objective: The course aims to equip students with comprehensive knowledge and practical skills in managing urban water systems effectively and sustainably. The scope spans water supply, sanitation, stormwater, groundwater, and urban drainage management. It incorporates key concepts in water-sensitive urban design, reuse and recycling of wastewater, climate-resilient infrastructure planning, and integrated urban water modelling. Emphasis is placed on understanding emerging urban water challenges, regulatory frameworks, and digital tools for decision support. Through hands-on sessions, case studies, and software exposure, the course objectives are: (1) To understand the integrated urban water cycle and its components; (2) To develop competence in water quality and infrastructure assessment; (3) To analyze risks and sustainability indicators in urban water systems; (4) To apply hydroinformatics tools for modeling and performance evaluation; and (5) To foster decision-making skills relevant to urban water management, policies, and climate adaptation strategies. 3. Course learning outcomes:  Understand and assess the urban water cycle and system interactions under climate change and urbanization.  Demonstrate practical knowledge in water quality, stormwater, and sanitation system design and management.  Use hydroinformatics and modeling tools for flood forecasting and system performance evaluation.  Integrate water-sensitive urban design principles and sustainability indicators in planning. 4. Text books and references: TB1. Water Supply Engineering, S. K. Garg (18th ed.), Khanna Publishers. TB2. Water Supply and Sanitary Engineering, G. S. Birdie & J. S. Birdie (8th ed.), Dhanpat Rai Publishing Company, New Delhi. R1: STORMWATER DRAINAGE MANUAL Planning, Design and Management, Drainage services department, Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. R2: Peavy, H. S., Rowe, D. R., & Tchobanoglous, G. (1985). Environmental Engineering. McGraw Hill Education (India Edition, 2013). R3: Garg, S. K. (2010). Sewage Disposal and Air Pollution Engineering: Environmental Engineering (Vol. 2). Khanna Publishers, Delhi. 5. [Method of conduct of the course]: The course will be conducted through a combination of interactive lectures, software-based tutorials, case study discussions, and hands-on modeling sessions. Emphasis will be placed on blending theoretical foundations with practical applications to address real-world urban water challenges. Students will engage in:  Lectures using multimedia tools to explain concepts related to the urban water cycle, supply, drainage, and quality management  Software training modules on stormwater modeling, urban flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics using tools such as SWMM, EPANET, HEC-RAS, and QGIS. Pilani Campus ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION  Group assignments involving real-world problem-solving, such as urban flood mitigation planning or rainwater harvesting assessment.  Guest lectures or webinars by industry/academia/government experts and municipal engineers to expose students to professional practices.  If possible, field visits (where feasible) to treatment plants, stormwater systems, or urban recharge zones for experiential learning.  Project-based evaluations including presentations, technical reports, and modeling outputs aligned with industry standards. 6. Course Plan: weekly schedule for 14 weeks with [3] lectures per week Module Week(s) Lecture Reference Learning Outcomes Module 1: Introduction to Week 1–2 [L1-L6] TB1, TB2 - Understand the structure and Urban Water Systems significance of the urban water cycle. - Identify social, environmental, and economic challenges in urban water management. Module 2: Urban Water Week 3–5 [L7-15] TB1, TB2 - Explain water sourcing, Supply and Sanitation distribution systems, and recycling strategies. - Evaluate water quality parameters and understand testing and treatment technologies. - Understand fundamentals of sanitation, sewerage, and urban drainage design. Module 3: Stormwater and Week 6–8 [L16-24] TB1, TB2 - Analyze stormwater drainage Groundwater Management systems and sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS). - Design recharge and rainwater harvesting systems in urban areas. - Examine groundwater challenges

Mudennavar (P4), Vipin Kr Saraogi (P6) Course Description: Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization 1. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory. 2. Text Books: T1: B.P. Course Description: This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using CMOS technology. Course No : EEE F411 Course Title : Internet of Things Instructor-in-Charge : Prof. Vinay Chamola Instructor(s) : none Tutorial/Practical Instructors: Manvendra Singh, Shubham Sharma and Manish prasad 1. Course Description: Introduction to IoT, Sensors and Actuators for IoT, Programming IoT end points, Communications and networking in IoT, Data management in IoT, Security issues in IoT, Emerging technologies. This course is discipline elective (DEL) for: Undergraduate level: B.E. (EEE), B.E (ECE), B.E. (E&I)/ dualites in those disciplines. For other discipline, it will be considered as an open elective (OPEL). 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: This module is designed to provide students with solid technical knowledge and skills to build Internet of Things (IoT) systems. Internet of things has evolved due to convergence of multiple technologies - embedded systems, sensor technology, real-time data analytics, machine learning etc. Traditional fields of embedded systems, wireless sensor networks, control systems, automation (including home and building automation), and others all contribute to enabling the IoT. This course comprehensively covers various technologies and tools used for enabling IoT solutions. Knowledge of various topics required for building IoT prototypes like sensors and actuators/ Communications and networking and data management is also imparted in this course. This course would also help the students understand the various IoT security challenges and solution to address them. The course will also give the students exposure to how various real world problems are being solved by IoT based solutions (like in applications for smart city, smart farming etc.). There would also be some hands on sessions where students would learn how to build and program IoT systems and make end-to- end solutions for different applications. Furthermore, assignments and projects in this course would help students build IoT prototypes and apply what they have learnt in the course to solve real world problems. 3. Course learning Objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: a. Understand and explain the fundamental concepts, architectures, enabling technologies, communication protocols, data-management techniques, and security challenges associated with Internet of Things systems. b. Design and develop IoT-based solutions by integrating sensors, actuators, microcontrollers, communication networks, cloud platforms, and data-analytics tools. c. Apply practical programming and system-integration skills to build, test, and evaluate end-to-end IoT prototypes for addressing real-world applications such as smart cities, smart agriculture, healthcare, and industrial automation. 4. Course No. : EEE F 422 Course Title : Modern Control Systems Instructor-in charge : Prof. Dheerendra Singh Team of Instructors : NA 1. Course Description: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so- called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments drawn from various engineering domains. 2. Scopes and Objectives After completing this course the students will be able to 1) Analyze various properties (E.g. stability) of linear and nonlinear dynamic systems 2) Design linear state and output feedback controllers in time domain 3) Design linear optimal controllers in both deterministic and stochastic domains 4) Design Kalman Filter and Extended Kalman Filter (widely used signal processing tool) 5) Design nonlinear state feedback controllers using backstepping algorithm 6) Simplify higher order LTI models to lower order ones 3. Course Description: Optical communication systems and components; optical sources and transmitters (basic concept, design and applications); modulators (electro- optic, acousto-optic and laser modulation techniques); beam forming; focusing and coupling schemes to optical repeaters; optical amplifiers; optical field reception; coherent and non-coherent light wave systems; fiber optic communication system design and performance; multichannel light wave systems; long haul communications; fiber optic networks. 2. Course No : EEE F435 Course Title : Digital Image Processing Instructor-in-Charge : Pawan Kamalkishor Ajmera 1. Course Description: This is the first course on digital image processing. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and discusses the various discrete transformations, which are extensively used in image processing. It then goes on to discuss the different image processing techniques such as image enhancement, automatic image classification, and recognition. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: Digital Image Processing (DIP) involves the use of computer algorithms to perform operations on digital images to improve their quality, extract useful information, or prepare them for further analysis. The main objectives of DIP include enhancing image details for better visual interpretation, restoring corrupted images, compressing image data for efficient storage and transmission, and analyzing images for applications like medical diagnosis, satellite imaging, and object recognition. Its scope spans various fields such as healthcare, agriculture, surveillance, remote sensing, and artificial intelligence, making it a vital tool in both scientific research and everyday technology. 3. Course Description: The course describes both theoretical and practical aspects of semiconductor fabrication technology. This course will take you on the journey of silica sand to silicon integrated circuit (IC), i.e., “making a chip”. Converting a single crystal of silicon into an IC requires several fabrication steps, such as epitaxy, oxidation, chemical vapor deposition, metallization, ion implantation, diffusion, etching, and lithography. All these process steps will be discussed. Further, the modeling of each processing step would be discussed in detail. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course is designed to provide an introduction to the basic principles of semiconductor fabrication and to discuss various processing technologies. Fabrication of semiconductor chips is a joint venture by electrical engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges across various disciplines. 3. Textbooks: TB: J. Plummer, M. D. Deal, and P. B. Course No : EEE F472 Course Title : Satellite Communications Instructor : Sainath Bitragunta Email: : sainath.bitragunta@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in 1. Course Description: Review of microwave communications and LOS systems; the various satellite orbits like GEO, MEO, LEO; the satellite link analysis and design; the communication transponder system like INSAT, INELSAT etc; the earth segment and earth station engineering; the transmission of analog and digital signals through satellite and various modulation techniques employed; the multiple access techniques like FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, DAMA, etc; the INSAT program; salient features of INSAT – systems and services offered; satellite services offered by INTELSAT, INMARSAT and future satellites like IRIDIUM etc; future trends in satellite communications. 2. Scope & Objectives of the Course: This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, or- bital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and link- budget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixed- assignment multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) and briefly explore random-access schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine satellite position/coverage for a given orbit. 3. Course learning outcomes Some of the key learning outcomes are stated below. CLO1. Explain the fundamental concepts, historical evolution, segments, and subsystems of satellite communication systems. CLO2. Analyze radio-wave propagation effects and orbital mechanics (LEO/MEO/GEO) and their influence on system and link design. CLO3. Design and evaluate satellite RF uplink/downlink link budgets, including noise and intermodulation considerations, using hand calculations and simulation tools. 1 CLO4. Apply and compare digital modulation, coding, and multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) for satellite systems. CLO5. Identify and evaluate VSAT, mobile satellite links, understand GPS/GNSS system ar- chitectures and their performance limitations CLO6. To understand, appreciate and analyze recent trends in satellite communications such as next generation non-terrestrial network/space-air-ground integrated network. 4. Textbooks: TB1. Satellite Communication Systems, Pratt, Bostian, and Allnutt, 2nd Edition, John Wiley & Sons, 2019. References: Ref1. Satellite Communications, Robert M. Gagliardi, 2nd Edition, Springer, 2012. Ref2. Satellite Communications, Dennis Roddy, McGraw-Hill Professional, 2001. Ref3. Satellite Communications Systems, G. Maral and M. Bousquet, 5th Edition, John Wiley & Sons, 2009. Ref4. Digital Satellite Communication, Tri T. Ha, 2nd Edition, MGH. 5. Course Plan: This undergraduate-level satellite communication course deals with the fundamentals of satellite communications. The course comprises six modules: M1) Module 1 consists of an introduction, historical developments, and research trends. M2) Module 2 covers satellite orbits, orbit elements, orbital effects, and Friendship7 spacecraft. M3) Module 3 comprises satellite link parameters, uplink, and downlink budget. M4) The fourth module consists of modulation, multiplexing, and error control coding. M5) The fifth module covers multiple access techniques. M6) The last module includes selected topics such as very small aperture terminal (VSAT), mobile sat (MSAT), the global positioning system (GPS), differential GPS (DGPS) and recent trends and advances. This course provides a requisite conceptual foundation of ML and contextual application of ML techniques for improving the performance of electronic systems. The course introduces the major approaches to ML such as supervised, unsupervised, semi- supervised, and reinforcement learning. The course also lays emphasis on various deep learning techniques and their application to various types of electronic systems/sub-systems (e.g. control-dominated systems, NLP systems, vision-based systems, communication systems, embedded systems, IoTs). Additionally, the course covers advance topics in ML such as multi- modal, multi-task learning as well as transfer learning. The course discusses the challenges in implementation of ML techniques, complexity analysis of the ML architectures for hardware implementation, efficient architectures, and various topologies used for implementation. Outcomes: • Students should be able to apply ML techniques to model, design, validate, and optimize embedded electronic systems in their area of interest. • Develop the skills and practical exposure in modeling, developing, and debugging ML- based systems. • Develop the foundation required to explore advanced topics of research in ML. Course Number : EEE G515 Course Title : Real-Time Embedded Systems Instructor-in-charge : G S SESHA CHALAPATHI Course Description : This course will introduce the general concepts related to real-time systems from introduction, to designing a real-time system (RTS). It will deal will a reference model of an RTS which can be applied to any RTS. It will also teach the scheduling algorithms, resource management techniques, issues in hardware and software design, Real-Time Operating System (RTOS), advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems. 1. Scope and Objectives: Real-time systems are those systems that require a deterministic upper time-bound for the execution of a job. With the proliferation of the embedded system, which is the heart of items ranging from common every day appliances to life-critical systems, a great deal of work has gone into the characterization and design issues of Real-time systems. The course focuses on the basics of Hardware design, advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems. Specifically we discuss the Operating system, Scheduling, Software techniques, Run-time environment, failure management algorithms, Reliability and Fault-tolerance of real-time systems etc. 2. Course Number : EEE G516 Course Title : Signal Theory and Optimization Course Instructor : Sainath Bitragunta Email: sainath.bitragunta@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in 1. Course description: Probability theory and random variables; joint, conditional, and marginal distributions; functions of random variables; moments, expectation, and statistical inequalities; introduction to random processes; stationarity, autocorrelation, ergodicity, and power spectral density; basic concepts of linear algebra: vector spaces, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations, spectral decomposition; matrix factorizations including SVD, LU, and QR; positive definite matrices; orthogonal projections in Hilbert spaces; introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization; Lagrange multipliers, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and numerical optimization techniques. 2. Scope and Objectives: The instructor presents the content of the course "Signal Theory and Optimization" in five modules. The first module (module-0) comprises preliminaries covering signals classification, definitions, properties, limitations, and applications. The subsequent module (module-1) consists of axiomatic probability theory and random variables, joint, conditional, and marginal distributions of random variables, first and second order statistics, Moment generating function, characteristic function, functions of random variables, and statistical inequalities, generation and simulation of random variables. The third module (module-2) mainly introduces stochastic processes, specifications, concepts such as stationarity, autocorrelation, crosscorrelation, ergodicity, energy, and power spectral densities. The fourth module (module-3) consists of basic concepts of linear algebra, namely, vector spaces, linear independence and dependence, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations (matrices), standard matrices (for example, positive definite and semidefinite matrices), matrix decompositions (for example, LU, and QR, Eigen _ Pilani Campus Instruction Division value decomposition (EVD), singular value decomposition (SVD)) and their uses, Hilbert spaces and norms, projections, inequalities, orthogonalization. The fifth and final module (module-4) consists of an introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and optimization techniques such as Lagrange multipliers, numerical optimization (non-convex) techniques. The objectives of the foundational course are to lay strong foundations for i) probability and random signals and related theory, ii) linear algebra, matrices iii) optimization techniques and their uses in communications and signal processing. 3. Course Outcomes: At the end of the course Signal theory and optimization, students learn useful mathematical and probability concepts, tools (transforms, matrices, optimization), and techniques to model several phenomena that occur in communication systems and networks, and analyze and design them better. Specifically, they learn the significance of signal theory, fundamental laws of probability, finding moments of random variables, modeling using random variables, and random processes and their applications. Furthermore, generation and simulation of random variables using software tools like MATLAB/Python are also one of the essential practical outcomes of this course. In addition to strong random signal theory foundations, students learn useful techniques of linear algebra and matrices, optimization, which are useful in understanding and analyzing machine learning-aided next generation communication networks. 4. Course Number : EEE G539 (3 2 5) Course Title : Modelling and Analysis of Electrical Machines Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Aditya R. Gautam (email id:aditya.gautam@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Practical/Lab Instructor : Vedant Vyas 1.​ Course description: Review of Rotating Electrical Machines, Element of Generalized Theory of Rotating Electrical Machines, Linear transformation and Reference-frame Theory, DC Machines, Three-phase Synchronous Machines, Three-phase Induction Machines, Special Machines, Introduction to motor parameters estimation and model generation using MATLAB 2.​ Scope and Objective: The objective of the course is to comprehend and analyse the steady-state, transient and dynamic behaviour of electrical machines using mathematical models, and also to familiarize the students about advanced modelling. The course will develop students’ understanding on modelling of electrical machines from conventional methods to advanced methods through generalized theory of electrical machines. Furthermore, the students will appreciate the scope and applicability of course with the help of hands-on practice using simulation tools and hardware setup, encouraging and strengthening their ability to approach and investigate important challenges of automation and e-mobility associated to research interests of industries and academia, for example, digital-twin, model predictive modelling and control, fault analysis, predictive maintenance, and advanced control. Course Code : EEE G549 Name of the course : Fundamentals of Optoelectronics Instructors : Prof. Rahul Kumar (IC), Prof. Navneet Gupta, Prof. V. K. Chaubey Lab Instructor : Deepak Pareek I. Course Description: This course introduces the principles, design, and applications of optoelectronic devices. The course begins with a description of the interaction of light with semiconductor materials in a p-n junction configuration. This includes the phenomena of absorption, electroluminescence, and stimulated emission. The distinction between direct and indirect semiconductor materials is noted. Basic devices are then described: photodiodes, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), semiconductor optical amplifiers, and laser diodes. Array detectors, including complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) and charge-coupled devices (CCD) arrays, and array LEDs are then introduced. Basic specifications and applications of each of these devices are described, including solar cells, imaging with array detectors, and LED displays. II. Textbooks and References: TB1: Optoelectronics and Photonics: Principles and Practices (2nd Edition) by S.O. Kasap. R1: Solid State Electronic Devices by Ben Streetman & Sanjay Banerjee. R2: Semiconductor Optoelectronic Devices by Pallab Bhattacharya. III. Course Objectives: • Understand the fundamental solid-state physics governing light-matter interactions in semiconductor materials. • Analyze the operation, design parameters, and performance metrics of modern optoelectronic emitters (LEDs, Lasers) and detectors (Photodiodes, Solar Cells). • Evaluate the engineering principles behind advanced display architectures, flexible electronics, and matrix-based image sensors. • Apply theoretical knowledge through hands-on computational modeling and simulation of optoelectronic device behavior. _ Pilani Campus AUGS/AGSR Division IV. Course No : Soft Switching Converter Technologies Course Title : EEE G554 Instructor-in-Charge : Rajneesh Kumar 1. Course Description: This course covers analysis of series and parallel resonant converters, load dependent properties of resonant converters with ZVS/ZCS boundary. Operation of these converters for Zero-current Switching and Zero-Voltage switching is discussed in detail. The concept of resonance is extended to analyze the soft switching mechanism of semiconductor devices Diode, MOSFET and IGBT to reduce the switching loss and possible mitigation of EMI. The zero-current- switching and the zero-voltage-switching quasi resonant switch cell is discussed for full bridge converter. Design example of zero-current-switching and zero-voltage switching class E-inverter is also covered in this course. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: a. Understand the concept of resonant tank network b. Analyze the dependence of ZVS/ZCS boundary on load resistance c. Design ZVS/ZCS switch cell for DC-DC converter d. Analysis of switching loss and EMI under soft switching 3. Text Books: 1. Fundamentals of Power Electronics” by Robert W. Erickson, Dragan Maksimović, 2nd edition, 2001 Kluwer Publication. 4. Course No : EEE G593 Course Title : Power Quality Instructor-in-Charge : Ashish Patel Instructor(s) : Lecture: Ashish Patel, Practical: Vedant Vyas. 1. Course Description: This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations, harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries. The objectives of this course are designed to help students to: a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact. b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems. c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and load voltage regulation d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination. e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable energy systems. Course No : EEE G595 Course Title : NANO-ELECTRONICS AND NANO-PHOTONICS TECHNOLOGY Instructor-in-Charge : V K CHAUBEY 1. Course Description: Semiconductor fundamentals for Nanotechnology, Introduction to low dimensional nano-structures and Quantum Mechanics ,Scaling and nanoelectronics, Nano electronic device materials and circuits, Strain engineering and high speed quantum electronic devices, Optical properties of nano-structures, Linear and non linear effects of optical materials and structures, Nano photonic devices, Electronic Devices based on nano structures in evolution of Silicon Base Devices, Integrated photo electronic devices and systems and its applications, New Trends in Nano devices and technology. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast moving technology involved in high-speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication systems in terms of nano structures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover, integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern technical aspects like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors, quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands-on-training in analysis/ simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software. 3. Course No : EEE G614 Course Title : Advanced Wireless Communications Instructor-in-Charge : Dr. Monolina Dutta Instructor(s) : Dr. Monolina Dutta 1. Course Description: Evolution of wireless cellular technologies to 5G and beyond, review of matrix and signal theory for communication applications, introduction to stochastic geometry for performance analysis of wireless networks, D2D communications- modeling and analysis, cooperative communications-buffer-aided relaying and performance analysis, modulation and multiple access techniques-NOMA, OTFS, OAM. Introduction to potential technologies for beyond 5G/6G communications: IRS, molecular communications, and AI in wireless communications. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: a) This course aims to introduce the students to the advances in wireless communications and expose them to the research options available for applications in the real-world implementation of the next- generation wireless networks. b) The course will introduce the students to current trends in the wireless industry with a specific focus on the 5G and beyond 5G communication networks. c) The course aims to equip students with tools for designing the engineering aspects of wireless communications. d) New techniques envisaged to be a part of the next-generation wireless networks, like D2D communications, NOMA, OTFS, and stochastic geometry applied to wireless communications, to name a few, will be covered to make the student industry and research-ready. 3. Scope and Objective: This course deals with the system-level design of embedded systems comprised of both hardware and software. It investigates topics ranging from system modeling to hardware-software implementation. This course also teaches analysis and optimization processes for supporting algorithmic and architectural design decisions. It also helps the student gain design experience through different case studies. The course emphasizes a top-down design methodology driven by bottom-up constraints. The topics covered will include co-design of hardware and software involving key aspects like partitioning, mapping and optimization. 2. Course Learning Objectives (CLOs) are as follows a. Analyze embedded system requirements and develop suitable hardware–software co-design solutions by applying system-level modeling, partitioning, and synthesis techniques. b. Evaluate and optimize hardware–software architectures using partitioning algorithms, mapping strategies, and performance estimation methods to satisfy design constraints such as speed, area, power, and cost. c. Design and implement hardware–software co-designed embedded applications using contemporary design methodologies and FPGA-based platforms to address real-world engineering problems. 2. Course Description: Dimensions, units, dimensionless ratios, hydraulic similarity and the testing of models, Continuity and Bernoulli's equations, fluid properties, Reynolds experiment, laminar and turbulent flow in pipes, major and minor losses in flow through pipes, Flow in pipelines between reservoirs, open channel flow, Pumps, flow and velocity measurement devices. 2. Scope & Objective: This course introduces the foundational principles of fluid mechanics and their practical applications in hydraulic systems used in water and wastewater treatment plants and sewerage networks. It covers the behavior of fluids in motion and at rest, emphasizing both theoretical frameworks and engineering applications. Topics include flow regimes, pressure losses, open channel flow, pump performance, and hydraulic modeling. Students will develop analytical skills to solve real-world fluid flow problems and design efficient hydraulic systems. 3. Flow in Pipes: Apply Poiseuille’s law for laminar flow pressure drop; Analyze velocity profiles and pressure loss in laminar and turbulent pipe flow; Use Moody diagram and Darcy’s law to determine friction factors. 4. Complex Pipe Flow Systems: Evaluate flow in non-horizontal and variable diameter pipes; Estimate minor losses due to expansions, contractions, and fittings. 5. Pipeline Flow Between Reservoirs: Assess head losses and solve problems involving series and parallel pipelines. 6. Open Channel Flow: Define hydraulic parameters like wetted perimeter and hydraulic mean depth; Use Chezy’s and Manning’s equations to calculate discharge and flow depth. 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 7. topics_text: Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division COURSE HANDOUT (PART-II) Date: 30 July 2026 Course Content Introduction to hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere and anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space), with chemical interactions, deterioration (pollution and degradation/depletion) and remediation processes etc., understanding of our environment its chemistry, current industrialized ecology, environmental biotechnology, emphasizing biotechnological tools, such as microbial, genetic, and biochemical mechanisms, pollution, and remediation, sustainable biotechnological interventions in waste treatment, bioenergy production, and pollution control, integration of biotechnology with environmental systems. In addition to part I (General handout for all courses appended to the timetable) this portion gives further details regarding the course. Course No. : ENVS F212 Course Title : Environmental Chemistry and Environmental Biotechnology Instructor-in-charge and other instructor : Prof. Bibhas R. Sarkar (IC), and Prof. B. Vani Course Description: The course will provide an overview of the different aspects of the environment and the chemistry integrally involved in it. Broad description of the constituents of the environment namely the hydrosphere, the atmosphere, the geosphere and the anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space) will be provided with emphasis on the chemical interactions involved in each of them in their respective formation, balanced existence, deterioration (pollution and degradation/ depletion) and remediation processes etc. The course will be essential to gaining an understanding of our environment and the chemistry behind the processes occurring within, with relevance to the current industrialized ecology. The course will also provide an overview of environmental biotechnology, emphasising biotechnological tools, such as microbial, genetic, and biochemical mechanisms involved in ecosystem function, pollution, and remediation. The course will cover sustainable biotechnological interventions in waste treatment, bioenergy production, and pollution control. It is designed to build a foundational understanding of how biotechnology integrates with environmental systems, enabling learners to address environmental degradation in the context of modern industrialized ecology. Course Number: FIN F414 Course Title: Financial Risk Analytics and Management Instructor-in-charge: Prof. Byomakesh Debata Team of Instructors: Prof. Byomakesh Debata 1. Course description: This course focuses on the concept of financial risk in modern finance. Despite market volatility and irrational exuberance, effective risk quantification and management remain crucial. Regulators have imposed safeguards to curb excessive risk-taking by financial institutions. As a result, risk management has become a core function in the finance industry. The course is designed to prepare students for the growing demand in financial risk management roles. Financial risk (which includes interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk and portfolio risk), Application of Asset price Theory, CAPM and Modern Portfolio Theory, Multifactor models of risk and return, Capital adequacy, BASEL Norms; Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision guidelines, Value at Risk (VaR), VaR from regulator perspective, Responsive VaR Model, Addressing VaR weakness, Back testing Concepts - Checking the Strength of VaR Model, Issues with the Standard VaR models, Risk Not in VaR (RNIV) to VaR migration of risk, Volatility Clustering, Quantifying and Modeling volatilities, Hedging techniques, Options Greeks, Managing Risk with Derivatives. 2. Scope and Objective: The three core focus areas dealt with in this course are (i) Risk Identification, (ii) Risk Measurement, and (iii) Risk Management, in the context of modern-day finance. The scope and objective of the course is to enable students learn essentials of financial risk management. The three core focus areas along with the functions and workings of financial institutions encompass the entire coverage of this course. To meet the stated objective of the course, a detailed course plan is designed which students can refer in section 6 of this document. 3. Course learning outcomes: a. Understand and classify financial risks such as interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk, and portfolio risk in modern financial markets. b. Course No : GS F211 Course Title : Modern Political Concepts Instructor-in-Charge : Dr. Veena R Instructor(s) : Nil Tutorial/Practical Instructors: Nil 1. Course Description:  Concepts of State, Nation, Rights and Duties, Civil Society, Democracy, Citizenship and Justice.  Ideologies of Modern Politics: Social Contractualism, Liberalism, Socialism, Communism, Maoism, Anarchism, Secularism.  Selected Readings from key texts of leading thinkers in the History of Modern Western Political Philosophy including Machiavelli’s Prince, Hobbes’ Leviathan, Locke’s Second Treatise of government, Rousseau’s Discourse on the origin of inequality, Marx and Engels’ Communist Manifesto. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: This Course introduces certain select concepts of Politics that are relevant to the Modern/ Contemporary period. The course helps in unravelling the contexts from which these concepts emerged through a study of ideologies as well as first-hand reading of key texts in the history of political thought. This course prepares the students to be informed active citizens. The design and its execution emphasize the comprehension of political thinking, the application of communication and analytical skills, and the understanding of human diversity. Modern political concepts enhance the knowledge of the political science discipline by offering the conceptual vocabulary along with various methods of inquiry. This course not only increases students’ knowledge of the history of classical and modern political thought but also enlightens them with the fundamental values and ethical issues contested in politics over time. This course informs about the alternative moral and ethical frameworks for (re)interpreting and evaluating contemporary political discourses. Scope: As an introductory course in Politics, this is based on lectures and reading texts. However, the students are encouraged to move beyond the textbook and familiarize with the research studies by eminent scholars. This course encourages to use critical thinking and evidence to understand and evaluate rival theories and interpretations. Accordingly, Students are expected to participate in the classroom discussions as well as initiate and moderate discussions on political issues that may have captivated their interest. This practice enables students to develop a critical understanding of various political discourses and equip them to address political theories and questions of political life and 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division values. Course Number : GS F224 Course Title : PRINT & AUDIO-VISUAL ADVERTISING Instructor-in-charge : SANGEETA SHARMA Team of Instructors : Ashutosh Sharma 1. Course description: The course is planned to give a comprehensive working knowledge of Advertising and Marketing communication and how they inter-relate. It offers modules, case studies and do-it your own assignment opportunities. The main feature of the course is that it is constantly evolving, keeping itself relevant to the needs of the advertising industry. Today’s student is expected to understand all the major marketing functions: advertising, its process, integrated marketing communication involving across multimedia: podcast/podcasts, newspaper, magazine, television, and via Internet. It aims to enable the students to familiarize the advertising communication process and how it works in relation to market and the consumers. 2. Scope and Objective: a. To prepare the students to learn advertising concepts and theories in practice d. To expose the students to the traditional and digital media for advertising e. To sensitize them about various ethical issues when planning and implementing advertising and promotional programs g. To underscore the implications of AI within advertising realm 3. Course Number : GS F232 Course Title : Introductory Psychology Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Tanu Shukla (tanus@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in, 6168-H) 1. Course description: Psychology as a science, Perception, its nature, determinants, and measurement; Biological bases of behaviour; Consciousness, Motivation, and Emotion; Learning and behaviour modification; Memory and forgetting; Thought processes, Problem- solving, and Creative thinking; Individual differences—Intelligence, Gender, Personality, Stress, and Coping; Social thought and Social Behaviour; with an emphasis on psychological assessment, behavioural data, research analytics, and evidence-based decision-making. 2. Scope and Objective: To develop a conceptual framework for understanding the human behaviour; relevance of psychology in daily life and its application in social, educational, industrial, personal and other spheres. 3. Course learning outcomes: CLO1. Explain the major concepts, theories, and principles of psychology, including the biological, cognitive, emotional, developmental, personality, and social foundations of human behaviour. CLO2. Apply psychological principles to analyse everyday individual and social behaviour, decision-making, learning, motivation, stress, and interpersonal interactions. CLO3. Compare and critically evaluate major psychological perspectives, theories, and empirical evidence to explain human thought, emotion, and behaviour. CLO4. Demonstrate an understanding of psychological research methods, ethical principles, basic research design, and the interpretation of psychological data. CLO5. Evaluate individual differences in perception, intelligence, personality, emotion, and behaviour using evidence-based psychological concepts and appropriate assessment approaches. CLO6. Integrate psychological knowledge to promote self-awareness, effective communication, well-being, problem-solving, and responsible decision-making in academic, professional, and social contexts. 4. Course No. : GS F233 Course Title : Public Policy Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Natasha Hazarika 1. Scope and Objective of the Course: The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the art and craft of policy analysis. This course covers theories, processes and techniques of public policy making, monitoring and evaluation. The course also covers the international agencies and the globalization of policy agenda. 2. Text Book: R.K. Sapru, Public Policy: Art and Craft of Policy Analysis, Second Edition, PHI Learning Private Ltd., New Delhi, 2011. 3. Reference Material- Books/Papers: Eugene Bardach and Eric M. Patashnik, A Practical Guide for Policy Analysis: The Eightfold Path to More Effective Problem Solving by. CQ Press, 2019. Book chapters, Journal papers, and newspaper reports will be given in advance as reading materials before each session. Students should be prepared to think out of box for maximizing their learning curve. 4. Course Format: The course format will be interactive with regular class discussions and several group exercises and presentations. Students are expected to prepare in advance with the help of reading material provided and through self-initiative. 5. Course Outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to understand the nature, scope and significance of Public Policy as a scientific activity; students will be able to analyse various contemporary public policies being made in India and elsewhere; through exposure to this course, students will gain the knowledge required for working in the public and private sector on various policy related issues. 6.
