Course No : GS F245 Course Title : Effective Public Speaking Instructor-in-Charge : PUSHP LATA Manasi Panwar (RS) Apoorv Kumar (RS) 1. Course Description Goals of Public Speaking, differences and similarities between Public Speaking and General Purpose Speaking, Role of Critical Thinking in Successful Public Speaking, Speaker’s Credibility; Different phases of Nervousness, dealing with Nervousness; Non- Verbal Communication, Using Body and Voice for communication, paralinguistic features; Using visual aids; Speech Writing and delivering- Effective Introductions and Conclusions; Speeches for Special Occasions; Team Presentations; Group Discussion and Job Interviews 2. Scope and Objectives of the Course The course aims to familiarize students with the art of public speaking and help them become confident, ethical, and effective speakers in academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to manage public speaking anxiety, construct logical arguments, organize speeches, and deliver presentations using appropriate content, structure, language, paralinguistic features, kinesics, and visual aids. The revised course also enables students to use AI-assisted tools in a limited and responsible manner for idea generation, outline development, rehearsal feedback, and slide improvement, without replacing independent thinking or original expression. Students will be encouraged to assess AI output critically for accuracy, audience suitability, bias, and ethical use. 3. Classroom Methodology The classroom methodology includes lectures, group and pair work, practical activities, guided rehearsal, and performance-based tasks. The course remains strongly practice-oriented and develops speaking skills through JAMs, extempore speaking, storytelling, parliamentary debates, group discussions, interviews, and presentation tasks. Video clips and model speeches will be used for illustration. In addition, selected classroom activities may include AI-supported speech brainstorming, AI-assisted audience adaptation tasks, and guided reflection on AI-generated feedback, while preserving the same teacher-led, practice-based format intact. 4. Text Books TB 1: Lata, P., & Kumar, S. (2007). Communicate or collapse: A handbook of effective public speaking, group discussion, and interviews. Prentice Hall of India. TB 2: Lucas, S. E., & Stob, P. (2020). The art of public speaking. McGraw-Hill. TB 3: Penn State University Libraries. (2026). Beyond the Podium: AI, Speech, and Civic Voice. Asia- Pacific Holdings Private Limited. Selected research readings on AI and public speaking pedagogy, including work on AI in public-speaking curricula, AI-based feedback, and delivery-focused AI activities. 5. Course description: Nature and dynamics of conflict; characteristics of conflict; theories of conflict; reasons and sources of conflict; value of conflict in social change; different approaches to addressing and managing conflict; conflict analysis through socio-economic class; class-based dimensions of conflict; culture and globalization perspectives; role of culture in propagating conflict; role of globalization in nation-state conflict; workplace and organizational conflict dynamics; conformity theories and conflict; power of communication; identity-based perspectives on conflict; AI, technology, and conflict resolution; algorithmic and digital dimensions of conflict; negotiation techniques; mitigation and resolution techniques; conflict management styles. 2. Course No ​ ​ : GS F313 Course Title ​ ​ : Marxian Thought Instructor-in-Charge​ ​ : Dr. Paul Mathew ​ 1. Course Description: This course aims to introduce undergraduate students to key concepts of Marxist theory. After beginning with a brief survey of the dominant narratives on inequality and exploitation, students will be introduced to the critique of bourgeois history developed by Marx and Engels, particularly in their writings on dialectical and historical materialism. In order to get a clearer view of how capitalism produces surplus value, Marx’s Labor Theory of Value and other related concepts will be read and discussed. At regular intervals, this conceptual framework will be applied to analyze cultural texts (films, advertisements, popular culture etc.) in order to develop analytical skills that surpass conventional wisdom in the study of social and economic structures. 2. topics_text: ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION First Semester 2026-27 Course Handout Part II Date: 1 August 2026 In addition to part I (General Handout for all courses appended to the Timetable), this portion gives further specific details regarding the course. Course Number : GSF 331 Course Title : TECHNIQUES IN SOCIAL RESEARCH Instructor-in-charge : Dr. Tanu Shukla (Tanus@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in, 6168- H.) [Team of Instructors] :[ ] (email, chamber no.) 1.​ Course description: Introduction to social research: nature, purpose, relevance, dimensions, and the research process. Quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, and triangulation. Social theory, ideology, positivist, interpretivist, critical, feminist, and postmodern perspectives. Research ethics and research design. Measurement, reliability, validity, scales, and sampling. Experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, and nonreactive research methods. Data collection techniques, questionnaire design, interviewing, content analysis, and secondary data analysis. Quantitative and qualitative data analysis, coding, concept formation, inferential statistics, and report writing. Research analytics and software applications: statistical analysis using SPSS and Jamovi; qualitative coding and thematic analysis using NVivo; bibliometric, scientometric, and science mapping using Graphica (e.g., knowledge network visualization and research analytics). 2.​ Scope and Objective of the Course: This course seeks to provide knowledge and skills relevant for conducting social science research. It will cover the entire research process from problem formulation, interpretation of data (both qualitative and quantitative) to evaluation of research study. The course will also address fundamental social science issues, reasoning and approaches that govern certain methodologies. This course would help students in acquiring skills to undertake social research studies based on primary and/or secondary data. ​ 3.​ Course learning outcomes: CLO1: Explain the philosophical foundations, paradigms, and methodological approaches of social research, and distinguish between qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods research designs. CLO2: Design ethically sound social research studies by formulating research problems, conducting literature reviews, selecting appropriate research designs, sampling strategies, and data collection methods. CLO3: Apply principles of measurement, reliability, validity, scale development, and sampling to develop rigorous research instruments for social science investigations. CLO4: Analyze quantitative and qualitative data using appropriate statistical and qualitative analysis techniques, including the use of software such as SPSS, Jamovi, and NVivo. CLO5: Evaluate and interpret findings from diverse research methodologies, including experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, content analysis, and secondary data research, to draw evidence-based conclusions. CLO6: Prepare and communicate research reports that demonstrate ethical research practices, critical interpretation of findings, and effective use of research analytics and visualization tools for scholarly dissemination. 4.​ Text books and references: TB1. Course No. : HSS F 227 Course Title : Cross Cultural Skills Instructor-in- Charge : PUSHP LATA Team of Instructors : Pradeep Bailwal (RS) Scope and objective of the course: 1. Providing insights into intercultural communication with powerful and deeply held views from multiple cultures. 2. Familiarizing the students how to undertake that critical self-reflection which may lead to better appreciation of the cultural diversity possessed by communities worldwide. 3. Bringing into the discussions, the experiences of intercultural communication, knowledge of the field of communication studies and mass communication, and perceptions of intercultural communication as a woman and as men from diverse ethnic, racial and cultural backgrounds. 4. Using AI to enhance cross-cultural understanding, communication, and adaptation through interactive learning and real-world simulations. Learning Outcomes After doing this course the students will be able to: 1. Understand cross-cultural communication and its different dimensions based on national cultures, as propounded by Geert Hofstede and Edward T. Hall, as well as comparative study of various theories developed later, by researchers like Trompenaars & Hampden-Turner. 2. Gain a comprehensive understanding of how and why cultural groups differ and the nuances of cross-cultural teams. 3. Develop sensitivity to cultural variations in thinking, feeling, and behaving and adapting the same for cross-cultural communication effectiveness. 4. Learn management and interpersonal skills to reckon, predict, and leverage cultural differences. 5. Develop an appreciation for the global mindset vis-à-vis Indian cultural identity. 6. Know more about diverse national cultures and countries from class projects and presentations. Course No. : HSS F334 Course Title : SRIMAD BHAGAVAD GITA Instructor-in-Charge : PROF. VINAY CHAMOLA Instructor(s): PROF. PRATIK NARANG 1. Course Description: This course introduces students the timeless wisdom spoken by Lord Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita and enables them to appreciate and apply those in daily life. Beginning with the fundamentals of the need to understand spirituality, the content includes science of soul, various types of yogic practices, viz., karma-yoga (action in God consciousness), jnana-yoga (philosophical research for truth), dhyana-yoga (meditative practice), astanga-yoga (eightfold yoga system) and culminates with bhakti- yoga (devotional service to God). Adopting a topical approach, the course also touches upon these subject matters: the most confidential knowledge, three modes of material nature, nature, enjoyer and the consciousness, divine and demoniac qualities, and the perfection of knowledge. 2. Scope and Objective: Meant for anyone who wants to make his or her life peaceful, blissful and perfect by aligning oneself to the principles set forth in Srimad Bhagavad Gita. The prime objectives of this course are to understand our relationship (sambhandha) with God, the process of reviving that relationship (abhidheya), and the goal of that process (prayojana). In this context, the 5 important subject matter isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala and karma are discussed in detail. 3. Course Learning Objectives Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: 1. Explain the principal philosophical concepts of the Srimad Bhagavad Gita, including isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala, and karma, and the relationship among them. 2. Differentiate and analyse the major paths of yoga—karma-yoga, jnana-yoga, dhyana-yoga, and bhakti-yoga—along with their purpose and practical significance. 3. Apply the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita to improve time management, stress management, concentration, emotional balance, self-discipline, decision-making, and overall well-being in academic and personal life. _ PILANI CAMPUS AUGS/AGSR DIVISIONS 4. Course Description An introduction to the ethical concepts, theories, and codes that govern professional life. The course traces the foundations of ethics and the profession, before applying this framework across business, management, education, engineering, and computing. 2. Scope & Objective: This course provides a formal acquaintance with the concepts and frameworks of ethics; recognize the codes of ethics relevant to the experience of being a professional and develops an understanding of the ethical issues relating to professions generally, and to business, management, education, engineering, and computing in particular. Course Description:  Introduction-A survey of the international politics since the 20th century; Rise of Nationalism; World Wars, Emergence of IR as a discipline and the nature of its subject matter.  Key Defining Events in IR: Creation of United Nations, Cold War, Fall of USSR, September 11, China’s entry into WTO.  Key theoretical frameworks: Classical IR thinkers and their location within the existing IR canon that include realism, liberalism, constructivism, critical theory, and Asian theory of IR.  Key Agents of IR: State, Empire, International and sub-national agents, foreignpolicy.  Key Structures in IR: State-system, Eurocentrism, Post-colonialism, Globalization, Security and Global Governance  Key Institutions in IR: International Society, International Diplomacy, Great Powers, Balance of Power, War, International Law and Human Rights Regime and the Climate Change Regime.  Assorted Themes: Global Health Regime- Pandemic and IR  India’s Foreign Policy: Locating India’s space in the contemporary global order: identifying the opportunities and Challenges (India-Pakistan-China), India and China in South Asia; India and United States. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: International Relations is the study of an international system that is constituted by territorial states who enjoy sovereignty over matters of vital interests to them. This course offers the history of the international system, its functioning, theoretical frameworks, and the nature of the changing relations between the states and non-state actors. This course offers a critical reflection and analytical understanding of key defining events and the topical issues that not only shaped but also confronted the existing international order. The course encourages students to engage in debates on the nature of international order as well as the responses to the challenges of the current international order. The course is designed to offer both the theoretical frameworks and critical reflections on the contemporary affairs. Moreover, the students will be able to make a clear perception of the relationship between the international relations as a discipline and the practice of world politics. Course No : HSSF349 Course Title : ECOCRITICISM Instructor-in-Charge : Susan Haris (susan.haris@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) 1. Course Description: Ecocriticism has found its place in the Indian academy only in the last twenty years or so. The course is intended to familiarize the learners with ecological, deep ecological and tinai critical principles and show them how these could be effective critical tools. The course gives a humanistic perspective on how ecology is a new paradigm in cultural and literary texts. The learners will be exposed to recent ecocritical concepts which will challenge conventional attitudes and values which are detrimental to the well- being of our planet. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 1. To introduce the learners to one of the major postmodern critical trends. 2. To familiarize the learners with some key ecocritical concepts. 3. To equip the students to create ecocritical documents in literary, cinematic and other artistic forms. 4. To train the learners in the application of the critical concepts to various cultural texts. 3. Text Books: Glotfelty, Cheryll and Harold Fromm. Eds. The Ecocriticism Reader: Landmarks in Literary Ecology. Athens and London: U of Georgia Press, 1996. Print. Alex, Rayson K, S. Susan Deborah and Sachindev P.S. Eds. Course Description: Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets, lattices and Boolean algebras; Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques; Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations, generating function, partitions; Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and Hamilton graphs. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math- ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc- tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design and analysis of algorithms. 3. Course learning outcomes Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to: CLO1. understand the basic process of mathematical reasoning CLO2. identify valid arguments and fallacies; CLO3. understand the structure of proofs of theorems in Mathematics; 1 CLO4. write valid mathematical proofs; CLO5. use powerful techniques for handling computing problems in Mathematics and Computation; CLO6. understand important structures having wide applications to sciences, computer programming and various classification problems.; CLO7. to create new relations with useful properties from a given relation; CLO8. to learn basic concepts of Graph theory. 4. Course No. : MATH F101 Course Title : Multivariable Calculus Instructor-in-charge: PRAMOD EYYUNNI (6070-G, pramod.eyyunni@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Team of Instructors : Balram Dubey, Devendra Kumar, Sangita Yadav, Gaurav Dwivedi, Trilok Mathur, Shailesh Trivedi, Jitender Kumar, Divyum Sharma, Rahul Kumar, Dhiraj Kumar Das, Shuchita Goyal, Sudarshan Santra, Deepak Bhoriya 1. Course Description: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss. 2. Scope and objectives of the course:  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses. 3. Course learning outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:  CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.  CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs.  CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion. SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division  CLO4. Develop a deep understanding of the gradient vector, including its geometric meaning, its relationship to level curves and level surfaces, its role in directional derivatives, and its use in linear approximation and sensitivity analysis.  CLO5. Compute partial derivatives using the chain rule and total differentials, and apply these tools to model changes in multivariable systems.  CLO6. Formulate and solve optimization problems involving multiple variables, both unconstrained and constrained, using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers.  CLO7. Compute multiple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems, including rectangular, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.  CLO8. Perform change of variables in multiple integrals and understand the role of the Jacobian determinant.  CLO9. Set up and evaluate line integrals (for work and circulation), surface integrals (for flux), and volume integrals, and interpret their physical significance in applied problems. 4. Method of conducting the course: The instructional approach for this course integrates theory, practice, and computational exposure. Core concepts and mathematical derivations will be introduced through classroom lectures, while tutorial sessions will be devoted to reinforcing these ideas through guided problem-solving and application-based exercises. To supplement in-class learning, three video lectures will be made available, showcasing the use of computational software (MATLAB) for visualization and problem-solving. Student learning will be evaluated on a continuous basis through quizzes, assignments, and examinations, ensuring both conceptual understanding and practical competence. 5. Textbook: TB. J. Hass, C. Heil, P. Bogacki and M. D. Weir: Thomas’ Calculus, 15th Edition, Pearson Education, 2024. 6. Reference Books: (i) RB1. E. Course Description This course presents the study of differential equations with the objective of introducing the classical methods for solving boundary value problems. It also serves as a basis for the applications of differential equations, Fourier series and Laplace transform in the various branches of engineering and sciences. Course description: Introduction to optimization; linear programming; simplex methods; duality and sensitivity analysis; transportation model and its variants; integer linear programming nonlinear programming; multi-objective optimization; evolutionary computation techniques. 2. Scope and Objective: Engineers, scientists, analysts, and managers often face the challenge of making trade-offs between different factors to achieve desirable outcomes. Optimization is the process of making these trade-offs in the best possible way. Over the years, optimization problems have become well-established and are encountered in the physical sciences, engineering, economics, industry, planning, and many other areas of human activity. The objective of this course is to familiarize students with standard methods of solving optimization problems. This course covers various aspects of optimization, including a description of techniques such as Linear Programming and Nonlinear Programming, and their applications in various engineering and science disciplines, including economics and finance. Multi-objective optimization, which addresses optimization with more than one objective, is also discussed. Additionally, the course provides a brief and informative overview of the non- traditional optimization technique, Genetic Algorithms. 3. Course Description: Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets, lattices and Boolean algebras; Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques; Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations, generating function, partitions; Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and Hamilton graphs. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math- ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc- tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design and analysis of algorithms. 3. Course No. : MATH F312 Course Title : Ordinary Differential Equations Instructor-In-Charge : BALRAM DUBEY, Email: bdubey@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in, Chamber No: 6067-B Instructors : 1. COURSE DESCRIPTION: Existence and uniqueness theorems; properties of linear systems; behavior of solutions of nth order equations; asymptotic behavior of linear systems; stability of linear and weakly nonlinear systems; conditions for boundedness and the number of zeros of the nontrivial solutions of second order equations; stability by Lyapunov's direct method; autonomous and non-autonomous systems. 2. SCOPE & OBJECTIVE: Ordinary Differential Equations frequently occurs as mathematical models in many branches of science, engineering and economy. For a mathematician confronted with such a model there are a number of issues to address and various approaches to choose from: Is the problem well-posed? Do you expect the differential equation to have a solution? If so, is there a unique solution satisfying the given initial or boundary conditions? Can you find an explicit, analytical solution? This is only possible in rare circumstances. Geometric or qualitative methods: These methods give insights into general, qualitative features of solutions and do not require solving the differential equation. Stability and dependence on parameters: Having obtained a solution by any method, we would like to know how the solution changes if we change the initial data by a small amount (stability analysis) and if we change parameters in the differential equation (parameter dependence). Course helps deeper understanding of the complicated models that are there in the real life. 3. Course learning outcomes: CLO1. Existence and uniqueness of ODEs of nth order CLO2. Linear and nonlinear behavior of system of ODEs CLO3. Applications of ODEs in real-world problems Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 4. Course No. : MATH F313 Course Title : Numerical Analysis Instructor-in-charge: Devendra Kumar (Email: dkumar@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in, Chamber No. 6067-M (NAB)) 1. Course Description: Solution of non-linear algebraic equations; interpolation and approximation; numerical differentiation and quadrature; solution of ordinary differential equations; systems of linear equations; matrix inversion; eigenvalue and eigenvector problems; round off and conditioning. 2. Scope and objectives of the course: Enables one to devise algorithms for the numerical solutions of mathematical problems. Also discusses the error analysis of different algorithms. 3. Course learning outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to: • CLO1. Explain the fundamental concepts of numerical analysis, including sources of computational errors, floating-point arithmetic, error propagation, and conditioning. • CLO2. Apply appropriate numerical methods to determine the roots of nonlinear equations and evaluate the convergence, accuracy, and efficiency of different iterative algorithms. • CLO3. Solve systems of linear and nonlinear equations using direct and iterative numerical techniques and analyze the stability and conditioning of computational methods. • CLO4. Construct interpolation polynomials using standard interpolation techniques and estimate interpolation errors for function approximation. • CLO5. Compute numerical derivatives and definite integrals using finite difference and quadrature methods and assess the associated approximation errors. • CLO6. Obtain numerical solutions of ordinary differential equations arising from initial value problems using single-step and multistep numerical methods. • CLO7. Solve boundary value problems using finite difference methods and interpret the numerical solutions obtained. • CLO8. Determine dominant eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices using numerical algorithms such as the power and inverse power methods. • CLO9. Apply weighted residual techniques, including the Rayleigh–Ritz, Collocation, and Galerkin methods, to obtain approximate solutions of boundary value problems and compare their applicability and effectiveness. SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 4. Method of conducting the course: The instructional approach for this course combines theoretical concepts, analytical problem-solving, and computational practice. Classroom lectures will introduce the fundamental principles, mathematical formulations, and derivations of numerical methods. Tutorial sessions will reinforce these concepts through guided problem-solving, analytical exercises, and discussion of practical applications. Selected numerical methods will be implemented using MATLAB to provide hands-on computational experience, facilitate visualization, and enhance problem-solving skills. Student learning will be assessed continuously through quizzes, assignments, laboratory/computational exercises, and examinations to ensure the development of both conceptual understanding and practical proficiency. 5. COURSE NO. : MATH F421 COURSE TITLE : Combinatorial Mathematics INSTRUCTOR IN CHARGE : KRISHNENDRA SHEKHAWAT (6067Q, Department of Mathematics) COURSE DESCRIPTION: Combinatorics is often described briefly as being about counting, and indeed counting is a large part of combinatorics. As the name suggests, however, it is broader than this: it is about combining things. Questions that arise include counting problems: “How many ways can these elements be combined?” But there are other questions, such as whether a certain combination is possible, or what combination is the “best” in some sense. This course presents the different methods to solve the counting problems. We will mainly focus on combinatorial approach instead of algebraic approach. SCOPE and OBJECTIVES: Combinatorics is a fascinating and a broad subject. It’s hard to classify Combinatorics, but a common theme is that it deals with structures that are, in some sense, finite or discrete. What sets Combinatorics apart from other branches of Mathematics is that it focuses on techniques rather than results. The way a Theorem is proved is of bigger importance than the statement of the Theorem itself. Combinatorial reasoning underlies all analysis of Computer Systems. It plays a similar role in Discrete Operation Research Problems and in Finite Probability. It is very much useful in the analysis of the speed and logical structure of Operation Research Algorithms to optimize efficient manufacturing or garbage collections. It has been proven an efficient tool for Graph Counting. COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES: The course focuses on different techniques related to counting problems. Course No. : MATH F428 Course Title : TIME SERIES ANALYSIS AND FORECASTING Instructor-in-charge : SUMANTA PASARI Instructor : Sumanta Pasari 1. Course Desccription: This course on Time Series Analysis and Forecasting covers introductory concepts of trend, seasonality, and cyclicity in time series data. It reviews extrapolative and decomposition models and smoothing techniques. Discussions include autoregressive error structure – auto-covariance and auto-correlation, ACF, and PACF. Linear stationary model analysis, such as AR, MA, ARMA is included along with error diagnostics. It includes Box-Jenkins time series analysis and linear non-stationary models, such as ARIMA, SARIMA, and ARFIMA. Finally, we study some models with stochastic variance – ARCH and GARCH. The course includes discussions on multivariate time series models and associated techniques. It necessarily involves the use of statistical software and programming languages for hands-on practice. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: This 4th level course introduces time series analysis and associated forecasting techniques, in which students will be equipped with various forecasting techniques and knowledge on modern statistical methods for analyzing time series data. The course reviews extrapolative and decomposition models, introduction to Box–Jenkins time series analysis, and ARIMA models. The remainder of the course considers various practical aspects of the principles behind modern forecasting techniques. Students will study and develop the ability to select appropriate model to carry out forecasting. A one-hour lab will be conducted every week. Students will learn how to explore and analyze different types of time series data using R programming. 3. Text Book: T1: Box, G. E., Jenkins, G. M., Reinsel, G. C., & Ljung, G. M. (2015). Course No. : MATH U101 Course Title : Multivariable Calculus Instructor-in-charge: PRAMOD EYYUNNI (6070-G, pramod.eyyunni@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Team of Instructors : Balram Dubey, Devendra Kumar, Sangita Yadav, Gaurav Dwivedi, Trilok Mathur, Shailesh Trivedi, Jitender Kumar, Divyum Sharma, Rahul Kumar, Dhiraj Kumar Das, Shuchita Goyal, Sudarshan Santra, Deepak Bhoriya 1. Course Description: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss. 2. Scope and objectives of the course:  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses. 3. Course learning outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:  CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.  CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs. SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division  CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion.  CLO4. Develop a deep understanding of the gradient vector, including its geometric meaning, its relationship to level curves and level surfaces, its role in directional derivatives, and its use in linear approximation and sensitivity analysis.  CLO5. Compute partial derivatives using the chain rule and total differentials, and apply these tools to model changes in multivariable systems.  CLO6. Formulate and solve optimization problems involving multiple variables, both unconstrained and constrained, using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers.  CLO7. Compute multiple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems, including rectangular, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.  CLO8. Perform change of variables in multiple integrals and understand the role of the Jacobian determinant.  CLO9. Set up and evaluate line integrals (for work and circulation), surface integrals (for flux), and volume integrals, and interpret their physical significance in applied problems. 4. Method of conducting the course: The instructional approach for this course integrates theory, practice, and computational exposure. Core concepts and mathematical derivations will be introduced through classroom lectures, while tutorial sessions will be devoted to reinforcing these ideas through guided problem-solving and application-based exercises. To supplement in-class learning, three video lectures will be made available, showcasing the use of computational software (MATLAB) for visualization and problem-solving. Student learning will be evaluated on a continuous basis through quizzes, assignments, and examinations, ensuring both conceptual understanding and practical competence. 5. Textbook: TB. J. Hass, C. Heil, P. Bogacki and M. D. Weir: Thomas’ Calculus, 15th Edition, Pearson Education, 2024. 6. Reference Books: (i) RB1. E. Course Description: This course covers the following topics: Mathematical preliminaries; Fluid statics and forces on submerged bodies; Integral relations for a control volume; Mass, Momentum and Energy Con- servation; Reynolds Transport Theorem; Differential relations for fluid flow, Analytical solution of Navier-Stokes equation; Dimensional analysis and similarity; Inviscid potential flows; Bernoulli’s Equation; Internal and external viscous flows; Basic compressible flows. 2. Course No.: ME F217 Course Title: Applied Thermodynamics Instructor-in-charge: Prof. Suvanjan Bhattacharyya Co-Instructors: Prof. Chennu Ranganayakulu Scope: The subject matter in this course covers the applications of thermodynamics. This course is designed to acquaint the students with the thermodynamics of power generating and power absorbing machines. The course discusses gas and vapour power cycles, boilers, combined cycle power generation, vapour compression and absorption refrigeration cycles, gas mixtures, psychrometry, and air-conditioning, building cooling/heating load estimation. Text Books: 1. Çengel Y.A. and Boles M.A., Thermodynamics; 8th Ed., 2015; Mcgraw-Hill Education. Reference Books: 1. Nag P.K., Basic and Applied Thermodynamics, McGraw-Hill Education, 2nd Ed., 2009 2. Nag P.K., Power Plant Engineering, McGraw-Hill Education, 4th ed., 2014. 3. Rayner Joel, Basic Engineering Thermodynamics, Person Education. 4. Arora RC, Refrigeration & Air conditioning, 1st Ed., Prentice Hall India, 2010. 5. Arora CP, Refrigeration and Air Conditioning; 3rd Ed. 2009; McGraw-Hill Education. 6. P N Anathanarayanan, Basic Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 4th Ed., 2013, McGraw-Hill Education Page 1 Pilani Campus Instruction Division Course Objectives:  To determine the power output and evaluate the performance of simple thermodynamic cycles for power generation technologies in terms of thermal efficiency.  To analyze and evaluate the performance of coal based or gas based power generations technologies.  To analyze and evaluate the performance of vapor compression and vapor absorption refrigeration cycle.  To analyze and evaluate gas turbine cycle with multistage compression with intercooling, multistage expansion with reheat and regeneration terms of its efficiency.  To estimate air conditioning requirements of a space using various air-conditioning processes. Course Plan Module 1: Vapor Power Cycles Learning Objectives  To analyze ideal Rankine cycle for a vapor power plant using T•s plot and evaluate thermal efficiency by applying first law and second law of thermodynamics.  To evaluate performance of Rankine cycle considering isentropic efficiencies of turbine and pump.  To represent the Rankine cycle processes on the Mollier diagram (enthalpy•entropy chart).  To analyze reheat Rankine cycle for a vapor power plant using T•s plot and evaluate its performance by applying first law of thermodynamics.  To evaluate performance of regenerative Rankine cycle using feed water heaters.  To study boilers their mountings and accessories. Learning Strategy: Text book Topics Chap/Sec Carnot cycle deficiencies, Simple vapor power cycle, Ranking Cycle, Actual vapor power cycle, Mean temperature of heat addition. Techniques for 10, TB1 efficiency improvement, Reheat and Regenerative cycles with open & closed feed water heaters. Combined cycle power plant and its thermodynamics. Combined Heat and Power. Page 2 Pilani Campus Instruction Division Module 2: Refrigeration Cycles Learning Objectives  To study simple refrigerators and heat pumps systems and the evaluate of their performance.  Analyze the ideal and actual vapor compression refrigeration cycle.  Evaluate the second law efficiency of vapor compression refrigeration cycle.  Introduce the concepts of vapor absorption-refrigeration systems.  To determine maximum COP of an ideal absorption refrigeration system. Learning Strategy: Text book Topics Chap/Sec Vapor Compression Refrigeration Cycle, Actual Vapor Compression Cycle, HeatPump, 11, TB1 Second Law Efficiency of Vapor Compression Cycle. Basic principle of a Simple Vapour–Absorption System, Comparison of vapour compression refrigeration systems with continuous vapour absorption refrigeration 11; RB3 systems, maximum COP of an ideal absorption refrigeration system, properties of ideal & RB4 and real refrigerant-absorbent mixtures, single stage vapour absorption refrigeration system with solution heat exchanger. Introduction to compressors. Module 3: Psychrometry Learning Objectives  Differentiate between dry air and atmospheric air.  To define and calculate the specific and relative humidity of atmospheric air.  To calculate the dew-point temperature of atmospheric air and to relate the adiabatic saturation temperature and wet-bulb temperatures of atmospheric air.  To determine the properties of atmospheric air using psychrometric chart.  To apply the principles of the conservation of mass and energy to various air-conditioning processes.  To estimate heating and cooling loads of a space to be air conditioned. Learning Strategy: Text book Topics Chap/Sec Psychometric Properties, Psychrometric Chart, Mixing of moist air, 14, TB1; Psychrometry of air conditioning processes. RB3 & RB4 Inside and Outside Design Conditions, Simple Summer Air Conditioning 13 & 14, System, Supply Air condition and flow rate, Apparatus Dew Point, Winter TB1; 30, Air Conditioning. Building Cooling Load and Heating Load Estimate. RB3 & RB4 Page 3 Pilani Campus Instruction Division Module 4: Gas Power Cycles Learning Objectives  To analyze Gas power cycles for a perfect gas using P•v and T•s plot and evaluate its performance using first law of thermodynamics.  To evaluate and compare the thermal efficiency of regenerative Stirling/Ericsson cycle with that of Carnot cycle.  To evaluate effects of multistage compression with intercooling, multistage expansion with reheat and regeneration on performance on a simple gas turbine cycle in terms of its efficiency.  To analyze combined cycle and binary cycle power plants using first and second law of thermodynamics and evaluate their thermal efficiency. Course description: Unconventional manufacturing processes and analysis, micro-manufacturing technologies, introduction to computer-aided manufacturing, CNC machines, CNC Part programming, additive manufacturing, modelling and simulation of manufacturing processes, surface technologies, related laboratory exercise and fabrication project. 2. Scope and Objective: This course introduces students to advanced manufacturing technologies for fabricating components across multiple length scales. It focuses on the challenges of machining difficult- to-machine materials and transforming them into high-value products. The course emphasizes hands-on learning through CNC part programming, CNC machine operation, additive manufacturing, and digital-to-physical manufacturing workflows. Lectures complement laboratory sessions by covering the fundamentals, process capabilities, numerical methods, and optimization techniques required for the analysis and development of advanced manufacturing processes. 3. Course No.: ME F317 Course Title: Engines, Motors, and Mobility Instructor In-charge: Prof. A R Harikrishnan Tutorial Instructors: Prof. Shyam Sunder Yadav, Prof. Chennu Ranganayakulu, Prof. Suvanjan Bhattacharyya, Mr. Krishnaram K K Course Description: The internal combustion engine (IC) is a heat engine that converts chemical energy in a fuel into mechanical energy, usually made available on a rotating output shaft. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. These engines are often used for the propulsion of a vehicle (i.e., automobile, truck, locomotive, marine vessel, or aeroplane), and other applications include stationary engines to drive generators or pumps and portable engines for things like chain saws and lawnmowers, etc. This course will introduce the students to system-level design concepts and the workings of internal combustion engines. Furthermore, electric mobility has become an essential part of the energy transition. This course focuses on the fundamentals of the technology behind electric vehicles. It will cover the contents such as the working principle of electric vehicles and delve into its key components, e.g. motors and power electronics, battery technology, charging technologies and future trends in the development of electric vehicles. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course has been designed to make the students familiar with internal combustion engines and electric and hybrid electric power trains. Text Books: V. Course No: ME F323 Course Title: Energy Storage Technologies Instructor In-Charge: Dr. Srinibas Tripathy 1. Course Description: This course introduces the necessity, classification, operating principles, and applications of various energy storage technologies used in modern energy systems. Mechanical, thermal, electrochemical, electrical, and chemical energy storage systems will be discussed with emphasis on their design, operation, performance characteristics, advantages, limitations, and practical applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy integration. The course also covers emerging storage technologies including advanced battery systems, supercapacitors, hydrogen energy systems, and phase change material-based thermal storage systems. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The objective of this course is to provide students with a strong understanding of energy storage technologies and their role in sustainable energy systems. The course covers fundamental thermodynamic, electrochemical, and mechanical aspects of energy storage systems along with their design considerations, performance evaluation, safety issues, and practical applications. The course also aims to familiarize students with recent advancements, technical challenges, economic considerations, and future prospects of modern energy storage technologies. The course also introduces Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) as a simulation tool for the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of energy storage systems, with emphasis on thermal management and flow behavior. 3. Course No. : ME F340 Course Title : Introduction to Sport Engineering Instructor-in-Charge : M. S. Dasgupta Practical Instructors : Mr Bhavesh Verma (SWD), Mr Ajay Shekhawat (SWD) 1. Course Description: The course essentially prepares engineering students to utilize their existing technical knowhow for sports applications. The specific topics will include, working with human and human movement patterns, qualitative and quantitative techniques for analysis of human movement. Sports performance measure and analysis. Anthropomorphy, Ergonomics and Task design. Computer application in sports, computerized performance measure. Sports surface and its impact on sports performance, surface testing methods. Sports and training equipment case study, business around sports 2. Scope & Objective: This is an introductory course to impart knowledge and skill set related to working with human in sports engineering application. Understanding human movement pattern and performance measurement. Understand, assess and analyze effect of equipment, sports surfaces and environment on sports performance. Use of ergonomic concepts, image processing, smart sensors and data analysis in sports engineering. Standard techniques of evaluation and testing of sports equipment and sports surfaces and appreciation of business around sports industry. 3. Learning outcome: Course Learning Outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Understand the fundamentals of human movement and apply engineering principles to analyze sports performance. Appreciate the role of ethics, human factors, and design considerations in sports technology. Utilize modern computing tools for motion analysis and performance evaluation in sports. Gain insights into sports infrastructure, surface design, and their impact on athlete performance. Explore the business, innovation, and marketing potential within the sports ecosystem from an engineering perspective. 4. Text Books: (T1) Sport and exercise biomechanics - P. Course Number: ME F415 Course Title: Gas Dynamics Instructor-in-Charge: Biswadip Shome (biswadip.shome@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Team of Instructors: N/A 1. Course description: This is a first-level course offered to advanced first degree and higher degree students to understand the essential concepts in compressible flows. The course contents include Introduction to Gas Dynamics, Basic equations for compressible flow, Flow with friction and heat addition, Normal shock, Quasi one-dimensional flow, Oblique shock, Prandtl-Meyer Flow, Potential equation for compressible flow, Linearized flow solution, and Hypersonic flows. 2. Scope and Objective: a. Introduce students to important concepts and mathematical formulations of Gas Dynamics b. Enable students to formulate and solve engineering problems in Gas Dynamics 3. Course Learning Outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, the students will have the following learning outcomes: a. Develop a broad understanding of the basic concepts and theories in gas dynamics b. Develop an in-depth understanding of various gas dynamic concepts such as flows with heat addition and friction, normal and oblique shock waves, Prandtl-Meyer expansion waves, Quasi 1D flow in nozzles and diffusers, Linearized solution theory and applications, and Hypersonic flows 4. Course No : ME F427 Course Title : Continuum Mechanics Instructor-in-Charge : Prof. Amit R. Singh 1. Course Description: Introduction to tensors, tensor algebra and tensor calculus. Kinematics of deformation (displace- ment, velocity, deformation gradient, material and spatial field descriptions, description of local deformation, linearized kinematics, kinematic rates), left & right Cauchy-Green deformation ten- sor, Cauchy-Lagrangian strain tensor. Traction and stress (first Piola-Kirchhoff stress, second Piola- Kirchhoff stress, Biot stress etc). Mechanical conservation and balance laws (conservation of mass, conservation of linear momentum, conservation of angular momentum, conservation of energy, work done by stresses and the principle of virtual work, BVP, IVP, calculus of variation). Constitutive relations (constraints on constitutive relations, frame indifference, objectivity, material symmetry, constitutive models for linearly elastic, hyperelastic solids and fluid flows). 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: This course will provide an introduction to continuum mechanics. It aims to develop in students the foundational mathematical rigor needed to understand advanced topics in solid and fluid me- chanics. 3. Textbooks: TB1. Continuum Mechanics for Engineers, G. T. Course Number : ME F428/ ME U428 Course Title : SMART MATERIALS Instructor-in-charge : Dr. Hemant Sharma (Chamber: 2219-J) Team of Instructors : Not applicable 1. Course description: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices. 2. Scope and Objective: This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus- responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research- oriented work in smart materials and structures. 3. Course learning outcomes: CO1: Explain the terminology, operating principles, physical mechanisms and characteristic behaviour of major smart-material families and smart structural systems. CO2: Interpret basic characteristic curves, experimental observations and performance data to describe the sensing and actuation behaviour of smart materials. CO3: Compare major smart-material families and identify suitable materials for simple engineering applications based on their capabilities, limitations and operating requirements. CO4: Investigate smart-material behaviour through guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews or project work, and communicate the resulting observations and findings. 4. Course No. : ME G511 Course Title : Mechanism and Robotics Instructor-in-Charge : Dr. Prateek Kala 1. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course is designed to provide an in-depth and holistic understanding of the technology and principles underlying modern robotics. Over the years, the demand for human-like machines capable of replacing or assisting humans in diverse and challenging work environments has grown significantly due to reasons such as efficiency, precision, safety, and the need to operate in hazardous conditions. In response to this need, the field of robotics has rapidly evolved and established itself as one of the most critical and promising areas of engineering for the future. The course aims to build a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students, focusing particularly on the mechanical aspects of robotic systems while integrating relevant knowledge from electronics, computer science, and control engineering. It will cover fundamental and advanced concepts related to mechanisms used in robotic systems, their unique characteristics, and detailed kinematic and dynamic analysis essential for design and development. Furthermore, students will gain insights into the design methodologies, practical implementation principles, and real-world industrial applications of robotics. The course will also explore current issues, trends, and innovations in robotics, enabling students to appreciate its impact across industries and prepare them for future technological advancements in this rapidly expanding domain. Text Book: (T1) Mittal R. K. & Nagrath, I. J., “Robotics and Control”, TMH, 2003 (Reprint 2010 or later). Reference Books: (R1) Groover, M. P., et al., “Industrial Robotics”, McGraw Hill ISE, 1986. Course Description: This course provides a comprehensive foundation in industrial robotic systems and robot control. Topics include principles of robot kinematics, statics, dynamics, and control; rigid body motion and coordinate transformations; rotation matrices, Denavit-Hartenberg parameters forward and inverse kinematics; Jacobian analysis, workspace and singularity analysis; trajectory planning and motion optimization; robot statics and dynamics using Euler–Lagrange and Newton–Euler formulations; control system for robot, independent joint control, computed torque control, and force control; end-effector and gripper design for robotic manipulation and precision assembly; sensor-integrated robotic systems; collaborative robotics; robotic work-cell implementation; and case studies and applications of industrial robots in intelligent manufacturing environments. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course provides fundamental, theoretical, and applied knowledge of industrial robotics and robot control with a strong emphasis on hands-on learning and industry-oriented applications. The course develops a rigorous foundation in robot kinematics, dynamics, motion planning, and control required for the modelling, analysis, and operation of industrial robotic manipulators. Students will gain practical exposure to industrial robotic systems used in modern manufacturing environments for robotic manipulation, precision assembly, collaborative robotics, and intelligent production systems. Laboratory sessions and project-based learning will focus on robotic manipulator programming, trajectory generation, end-effector design, sensor-integrated robotic systems, and robotic work-cell implementation using industrial-grade platforms. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Apply principles of robot kinematics, dynamics, and control to model and analyze industrial robotic manipulators. CO2 Design and implement motion planning and control strategies for industrial robotic tasks such as pick-and- place, assembly, and material handling. CO3 Design and deploy sensor-integrated robotic work cells for real-world manufacturing applications with closed-loop control. CO4 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical robotics problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions. _ Pilani Campus ACADEMIC GRADUATE STUDIES AND RESEARCH DIVISION 3. Course Description This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of molding methods used for plastic components in the manufacturing of electronic components. It will introduce students to different molding techniques used for plastic components, and equipment, process considerations, and applications in the electronics industry. The second module provides an overview of the different materials, characterization and testing procedures, and environmental safety considerations in the electronic industry. In the third and fourth modules, students will be exposed to different plastic- moulding processes used in the fabrication of electronic components. The last module will provide basic design aspects related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould for fabricating electronic components. Through a strong focus on experimental exposure and industry case studies, students will develop practical insights into advanced manufacturing systems used in the electronics industry. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course This course introduces theoretical, analytical, and practical knowledge of plastic materials used in the electronic industry, as well as the manufacturing methods for plastic components. It provides students with basic knowledge of advanced casting methods for fabricating plastic components for the electronics industry. It enables learners to understand the principles of various advanced casting methods, the casting machines used, the mechanisms of these processes, the parameters involved, and basic design aspects related to mould. Additionally, this course provides industrial/practical exposure to industrial component development and various application areas with case studies. 3. CO2 Selection of appropriate materials for the electronic industry. CO3 Design and fabricate different plastic components using moulding processes. Course Description This course provides a comprehensive understanding of advanced computer-aided design (CAD) and digital product development techniques used in modern engineering design and manufacturing. It covers geometric modelling of parametric curves, surfaces, and Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS), along with geometric transformations, mass property evaluation, and product data exchange standards for seamless CAD interoperability. The course intro- duces Design of Experiments (DoE) for design optimisation and provides extensive hands-on training in basic and advanced Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) based on the ASME Y14.5 standard using commercial CAD software. Students will also explore the fundamentals of generative design, topology optimisation through industrial case studies, and the principles and applications of additive manufacturing, enabling them to design innovative, lightweight, and manufacturable engineering products. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course The course aims to develop knowledge and practical skills in advanced CAD, geometric mod- elling, topology optimisation, and additive manufacturing techniques. It enables students to apply geometric modelling, GD&T (ASME Y14.5), generative design, and modern engineering software to design, analyse, and validate innovative and manufacturable engineering products. Apply ASME Y14.5 concepts to communicate functional dimensional and geomet- ric requirements; CLO4. Formulate and interpret generative-design and topology-optimization problems; 1 CLO5. Course Description: The course has wide-ranging application in Engineering structures, Machine tool structures, metal forming, and cold working. The studies deal with the determination of stresses and displacements in common structural forms beams, shafts, shells etc. subjected to external forces. Course Number : MEL G623 Course Title : ADVANCED VLSI DESIGN Instructor-in-charge : PRASHANT KUMAR 1. Course description: The field of Digital Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits has gone through dramatic evolutions and changes. This course builds on the previous course MEL G621 VLSI DESIGN. It is intended to give a detailed knowledge and experience in the design of advanced VLSI circuits and chips in todays and future nano-scale CMOS technologies. Design of high-performance digital systems, failure issues, and remedies of problems. Topics will focus on current issues, including: wiring resistance and how to deal with it, power and Ground noise and regulation, clock (or asynchronous) system design and how to minimize clocking overhead, high-speed I/O design, energy minimization, including leakage control. Major VLSI design challenges are followed by careful treatment of several versatile digital and mixed analog-digital circuit building blocks frequently utilized in VLSI chips. 2. Scope and Objective: The development of digital technology over the past 50 years has revolutionized the design and performance of everything from mobile phones to cars and entertainment systems; and engineers continue to enhance the performance of these devices. Recent developments in nanotechnology promise further large increases in processing power with lower power requirements, and will open up a whole new world of applications for digital techniques. The course aims to learn new techniques to keep up-to-date with developments in an industrial and/or research setting, and will have hands-on experience of the different stages of the design of a modern digital system. 3. Course learning outcomes: Students will develop an understanding of common design and timing issues/challenges in digital systems. They will be introduced to high-speed/low-power circuit logic/ power minimization techniques, as well as wiring models used in digital systems. Additionally, they will learn about the clock system design and various noise sources that can interfere with these systems. 4. Text books and references: TB: J. M. Rabaey, A. Course Number : MEL G624 Course Title : Advanced VLSI Architectures Instructor-in-charge : Dr. Govind Prasad Team of Instructors : Prof. Chandra Shekhar, Dr. Govind Prasad 1.​ Course description: The course explores advanced VLSI processor architectures, their implementation strategies (microarchitectures) and associated memory hierarchies and their microarchitectures for high-performance system design. It also covers the various techniques utilized to leverage parallelism at hardware, application and compiler levels. Students will gain an understanding of how (beyond instruction-level parallelism) data-level parallelism, thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism can be exploited to architect and implement different processing cores e.g.: Vector Processors, SIMD processors and Multimedia processors, Graphical Processing Units (GPU) and Multi-core processors, Domain Specific Processors, and Memory hierarchy organizations for the above processors. The course also explores the emerging research directions in VLSI processor design and system architectures. 2.​ Scope and Objective: The objective of the course is to understand and gain an in-depth view of Advanced VLSI Architectures, specifically to study various processor architectures, associated microarchitectures, and memory organizations that have evolved to exploit different types of parallelism to increase processor performance. The scope of the course covers the following in detail: a.​ Study of advanced processor architectures and associated implementation techniques (microarchitectures) and memory organization techniques b.​ This includes the study of Vector, SIMD, GPU, and Domain Specific architectures and implementations c.​ Study of architectures and implementations that exploit thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism via multi-processing (includes multicore processors) d.​ Study of memory hierarchy design for CPUs, vector processors, GPUs, and application domain-specific processors 3.​ Course learning outcomes: a.​ Explain the advantages of CORDIC in hardware implementation, especially in terms of multiplier-less architecture, low power, and area efficiency. b.​ Analyze the design principles of advanced VLSI processor architectures and their microarchitectural implementation strategies for high-performance computing systems. c.​ Evaluate various memory hierarchy designs and optimizations, including their microarchitectural aspects, in the context of different processor types. d.​ Apply concepts of parallelism—such as instruction-level, data-level, thread-level, and task-level parallelism—to optimize system performance. e.​ Design architectural solutions using specialized processing units such as SIMD processors, vector processors, multimedia processors, GPUs, multi-core systems, and domain-specific accelerators. f.​ Explore contemporary research trends and emerging technologies in VLSI processor and memory system architecture to identify potential areas for innovation. 4.​ Textbooks and references: TB1. topics_text: Pilani Campus AUGSD/AGSRD Division FIRST SEMESTER 2025-2026 Course Handout Date 01/08/2026 Course No: MEL G625 Course Title: Advance Analog and Mixed Signal Design Instructor-in- Charge: Neeraj Mishra 1. Course description: Mixed signal blocks design issues,, design of high resolution, speed Comparators,, design of Active Mixers-balanced/ unbalanced,, Data Converters Architectures, CMOS multipliers , dividers and modulators , filters- active/ passive/ switched capacitor, Signal Conditioning and sensor associated circuits, Frequency Synthesizers, Phase Locked Loop, Power Management Circuits, Integrated Voltage Regulators, Energy Harvesting Circuits, Analog Testing, Analog layouts, noise issues, emerging trendshigh 2. Scope and Objective: This course is designed to provide in-depth knowledge and hands-on expertise in designing advanced analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits with a focus on modern CMOS technologies. The course aims to bridge the gap between analog fundamentals and practical design of performance-critical blocks such as Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs), oscillators, and Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs). It equips students to analyze, architect, and implement key mixed-signal blocks considering design trade-offs, non-idealities, and layout constraints. Emerging trends such as energy harvesting, sensor interface circuits, and digitally assisted analog systems are also discussed to build readiness for research and industrial innovation. 3. Course learning outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, the students will be able to: a. Analyse and Design high-resolution, high-speed comparators, mixers, and signal conditioning blocks for mixed-signal interfaces. b. Architect and Evaluate various ADC and DAC topologies based on speed, resolution, power, and area metrics. c. Design and Simulate PLLs and oscillator-based clock generation systems with attention to phase noise, jitter, and loop stability. d. Implement of Biasing Circuits and Optical/Wireline Receiver Transmitter circuits. Pilani Campus AUGSD/AGSRD Division e. Understand and Apply analog layout methodologies, matching principles, and noise-aware design techniques. f. Demonstrate Proficiency in using industry-grade tools (e.g., Cadence) to model, simulate, and layout mixed-signal circuits. 4. Text books and references: There is no single reference for this. It will be based on multiple journal articles and books that will be shared along with the relevant lectures. TB1. RF Microelectronics, B. Razavi, 2nd Ed BRB1. Design of CMOS phase-locked loops: from circuit level to architecture level, Behzad Razavi, 2020/1/30, Cambridge University Press RB1. CMOS Mixed Signal Circuit Design, R. Jacob, Baker, IEEE Press. RB2. Analog-to-Digital Conversion, 4th Edition Marcel J.M Pelgrom. RB3: CMOS Circuit Design, Layout and Simulation – R. J. Baker, 3nd Edition, Wiley-IEEE. RB4: Analog Design Essentials Hardcover – 31 May 2006 by Willy M. C. Sansen. RB5: IEEE ISSCC/CICC/AISSCC/ESIRCC conferences papers and IEEE JSCC/TCAS-I/II, research papers related to topics. 5. Method of conduct of the course This course follows a design-centric and research-driven pedagogy, aimed at cultivating both analytical depth and practical proficiency in analog and mixed-signal design.  Lecture Sessions will focus on conceptual clarity, design trade-offs, and architecture-level intuition using real-world mixed-signal systems as case studies. Select sessions will be used for dissecting key blocks such as PLLs, ADCs, comparators, mixers, and voltage regulators.  Research Paper Discussions: Students will regularly read, present, and critique seminal and recent research papers from IEEE JSSC, TCAS, and ISSCC to stay aligned with state-of-the-art trends. Discussions will emphasize circuit innovation, design methodologies, and practical constraints.  Hands-on Lab Sessions will be conducted using industry-standard EDA tools (e.g., Cadence, Spectre, Virtuoso) to implement and simulate analog and mixed-signal building blocks. Students will perform schematic-level design, corner simulations, layout practices, and post-layout verifications. Pilani Campus AUGSD/AGSRD Division  Mini Projects and Design Challenges: Learners will undertake short design assignments focused on specific circuit blocks (e.g., comparator, VCO, LDOs BGRs), progressively leading to a final design project.  Collaborative Learning will be encouraged through team-based design reviews, lab debugging, and peer feedback on presentations and reports. This method ensures that students develop a deep understanding of design principles while also acquiring practical experience in implementing and validating real circuits, preparing them for research, industry, or further academic pursuits. 6. Course No. : MF F315 Course Title : AUTOMATION AND CONTROL Instructor-in-charge : PRATEEK KALA 1. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course is intended to a comprehensive knowledge of the technology related to Mechatronics and Automation. The necessity of integrating and embedding electronics and microprocessor into mechanical systems have been long felt, due to rapid progress in microprocessor computer based technology, in domestic products to manufacturing systems. Mechatronics is a recently defined engineering field that builds on the traditional mechanical engineering studies, combines it with technologies from the electrical, electronics, computer and control fields, using techniques such as simultaneous engineering to provide solutions in manufacturing applications. Also, mechatronics has been applied to manufacturing and other industrial automation: robotic automation found in car automated production lines, such as welding, and assembly line in computer integrated manufacture etc. Thus, the manufacturing system is greatly enhanced by the application of mechatronics. This course will develop overall background of the student in interdisciplinary mechatronic technology and a broad introduction to the issues encountered and techniques required in developing mechatronic products and automation systems. 2. Course No : MF F418 Course Title : Lean Manufacturing Instructor-in-Charge : Abhijeet K. Digalwar 1. Course Description: Fundamentals of continuous improvement, value-added and waste elimination, elements of lean production: small lot production, setup time reduction, maintaining and improving equipment, pull production systems, focused factories and group technologies, work cells and cellular manufacturing, standard operations, quality of design, systems for eliminating defects, simplified production planning and control systems: scheduling for smooth flow, synchronizing and balancing process, planning and control in pull production, beyond the production systems: managing the supply chain, activity based costing, performance measurement. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: In factories around the globe, Toyota consistently raises the bar for manufacturing, product development and process excellence. The result is an amazing business success story: steadily taking market share from price- cutting competitors, earning far more profit than any other automaker, and wining the praise of business leaders worldwide. With a market capitalization greater than the value of General Motors, Ford and Chrysler combined; Toyota is the world’s most profitable automaker. Toyota’s well known “secret weapon” is lean manufacturing – the revolutionary approach to business processes that it invented in the 1950’s and has spent decades for perfecting. Today business around the world is attempting to implement Toyota system to maintain competitive advantage. But are they? The course explains Toyota’s unique approach to Lean manufacturing, that drive Toyota’s quality and efficiency obsessed culture. You will valuable insights that can be applied to any organization and any business process, whether in services or manufacturing. You will discover how the right combination of long- term philosophy, processes, people and problem solving can transform your organization into a lean, learning enterprise – the Toyota way. At the end of this course, the students will be able to understand the importance of lean manufacturing / The Toyota Way as a strategic weapon, the students will be able to understand the World –Class power of the Toyota way 3. Scope & Objectives of the Course: The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insight into the application of various supply chain modelling approaches and empirical analysis for evidence driven decision making in supply chain. The objectives of the course are: • To introduce concept of decision making on the basis of multiple experts’ opinion on various different supply chain problems, practices and strategies. • To develop skill sets to analyze the qualitative data with a focus on empirical modelling for data driven decisions in supply chain. • To develop model for life cycle analysis for measuring environmental sustainability in supply chain. • To understand and analyse the various aspects of digital supply chain, cultural implications and their impact on supply chain performance. 2. Course description: Human-centered innovation, Design thinking (DT), consumer needs, creativity for new ideas/products (or re- design products) for solving problems, DT process’ stages– inspiration, ideation & implementation, DT tools – stakeholder map, user persona, Hook’s canvas, empathy map, AEIOU model, PoV, problem statement, stakeholder wish list, SCAMPER, prototyping & testing, MVP or minimum viable product, business model/canvas & business ecosystem. The pedagogical focus will be on hands-on approach to learning. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The objective is to develop knowhow and skills that promote human-centered approach to innovation through design thinking (DT). It will aim to develop understanding of consumer needs & using creativity for new ideas/products (or re-design products) for solving problems. Course will also help understand prototyping, testing of new ideas & see the context of the larger ecosystem. Focus will be on understanding design thinking concept and tools for effective innovations that can solve consumers’ needs holistically. Design Thinking process is laid across 3 stages- inspiration, ideation and implementation for new product development or re-design & concepts like MVP or minimum viable product, business model/canvas & business ecosystem will be also covered.
