Course No : MPBA G503 Course Title : Marketing Instructor-in-Charge : ANIL BHAT Tutorial/Practical Instructors: 1. Course Description: This basic course in marketing is designed to familiarize students with the strategic and tactical decision making process in marketing that deals with the fundamental goal of creating, communicating and delivering value to the customer. This requires a professional knowledge of market drivers, competitors’ capabilities, technological trends and the market dynamics of value. The focus will be on the imbibing the skills of uncovering market opportunities by asking certain strategic questions. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: On successful completion of this course, participants will be able to critically analyze and intelligently draw inference about the marketing strategies of organizations. Through an intensive assignment an effort will be made to develop the necessary skills for crafting a typical marketing plan grounded in real world data. Finally, awareness of tools available to marketing managers to facilitate planning and decision-making would be one of the gains from the course. Students are encouraged to bring some of the topical issues of contemporary concern in marketing to the classroom for discussion. Students will also be expected to imbibe path-breaking classic marketing literature in a group setting through group discussions for a sound academic base. A number of journal articles will be discussed in this course to give the course its academic rigor. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis on “learning by doing” through regular discussion of 6-7 Harvard Business Review cases as well as through a group marketing project assignment. 3. Course Number : MPBA G504 Course Title : Managing People & Organization Instructor-in-charge : Dr. Jayashree Mahesh Team of Instructors : NA 1. Course description: The course studies human behavior in organizations at three levels: individual, group, and organizational systems. It examines variables and key concepts related to individual attitudes, motivation, and leadership, along with group dynamics, organizational structure, and change management, while also covering the strategic role of HRM in attracting, developing, motivating, and retaining talent through recruitment and selection, training and development, performance management, employee engagement, compensation, and talent management. 2. Scope and Objective: In the contemporary time, organizations across the world are facing economic and social consequences of global economic pressures and globalization. Under such scenario, they encounter many challenges and get various opportunities as well. Moreover, management of these challenges and opportunities has become crucial which essentially relies on an understanding of human behavior. The success of any organization in today's dynamic and volatile business environment is dependent upon the motivation and commitment of its employees. It is in this context the significance of organizational behavior comes into play. As people from diverse backgrounds and with different cultural values have to work together in the global economy, the study of organizational behavior assumes greater importance and relevance. This course focuses on the fundamental theories of behavior in organizations and managing employees in organizations with the objective of equipping students with the necessary concepts, tools, and techniques for understanding behavior in organizations, this course attempts to unfold human behavior at three levels (the individual, the group, and the organization). This course involves active learning and develops students' foundation against which the competencies required to create a successful organization can be built and developed. 3. Course learning outcomes: By the end of the course the students are expected to:  CLO1. Comprehend the fundamental concepts in organizational behavior and human resource management and the tight coupling between them  CLO2. Apply concepts of organization behavior to their everyday workplace context  CLO3. Apply frameworks for managing talent at their workplace  CLO4.Comprehend the pros and cons of different organizational structures and apply them, as needed at their workplace. 1  CLO5.Comprehend the importance of organizational culture and change management strategies 4. Text books and references:  TB1. Organizational Behavior by Stephen P. Robbins & Timothy A. Judge. Pearson Education, Updated 18th Edition, 2022  TB2. Dessler Gary & Varkkey, Biju. Course description: Probability and Probability Distributions, Characteristics of Probability Distributions, Some Important Probability Distributions, statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing; ANOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA, the linear regression model (two-variable model, multiple regression, functional forms, dummy variables); regression analysis in practice (model selection criteria and tests, multicollinearity, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation), simultaneous-equations models. Statistical package 'R' will be used in this course. 2. Scope and Objective: This course serves as an introductory exploration of statistical analysis and fundamental econometrics, wherein the principles of economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference are employed to examine business phenomena. The curriculum encompasses a review of probability distributions, statistical inference, estimation, and hypothesis testing. It also covers analysis of variance (ANOVA), analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), and introduces multiple regression analysis, which remains the most widely utilized statistical technique within the field of econometrics. The latter part of the course addresses various practical considerations related to linear regression models, including the use of dummy variables, alternative functional forms, and the implications of violating classical regression assumptions. Students will engage in the study and application of regression analysis to diverse data sets, thereby gaining familiarity with core concepts such as the estimation of economic parameters, forecasting business outcomes, and conducting statistical inference. A weekly two-hour laboratory session will be conducted, during which students will learn to explore and analyze different types of economic data using R programming. This component aims to develop proficiency in advanced statistical and econometric techniques through practical applications in R. 3. Course learning outcomes: By the end of this course, students should be able to: CLO1:Apply statistical and econometric models to estimate relevant business parameters, predict economic outcomes, and test hypotheses using quantitative data. CLO2:Understand the fundamental assumptions underlying the classical linear regression model and identify and address potential violations, such as autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity. CLO3:Develop and sustain a foundational knowledge of econometrics that will serve as a basis for further study in business analytics and advanced statistical methodologies. 4. As big data problems become more prevalent for businesses, this module introduces the basics of databases. After successful completion of the course, students will be able to learn why database management is essential, analyze the data requirements of a business scenario and represent these requirements utilizing entity-relationship (ER) diagrams, translate an ER diagram into normalized tables for a relational database management system, and write simple and relatively complex data retrieval queries. topics_text: BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHONOLOGY AND SCIENCE, PILANI Pilani Campus INSTRUCTION DIVISION FIRST SEMESTER 2026-27 Course Handout Part II Date: 3/08/2026 In addition to Part-I (General Handout for all courses appended to the timetable), this portion gives further specific details regarding the course. Course No. : MPBA G515 Course Title : PRESCRIPTIVE ANALYTICS WITH MATHEMATICAL PROGRAMMING Instructor-in-charge : PROF RAJESH MATAI 1. Scope & Objective: Prescriptive analytics is the third and final phase of business analytics, which also includes descriptive and predictive analytics. Referred to as the "final frontier of analytic capabilities", prescriptive analytics entails the application of mathematical and computational sciences and suggests decision options for how to take advantage of the results of descriptive and predictive phases. The first stage of business analytics is descriptive analytics, which still accounts for the majority of all business analytics today. Descriptive analytics looks at past performance and understands that performance by mining historical data to look for the reasons behind past success or failure. Most management reporting – such as sales, marketing, operations, and finance – uses this type of post- mortem analysis. The next phase is predictive analytics. Predictive analytics answers the question of what is likely to happen in the future. This is where historical data is combined with rules, algorithms, and occasionally external data to determine the probable future outcome of an event or the likelihood that a situation will occur. The final phase is prescriptive analytics, which goes beyond predicting future outcomes to suggest actions to benefit from those predictions and show the implications of each decision option. While the term prescriptive analytics was first coined by IBM and was later trademarked by Texas-based company Ayata, the underlying concepts have been around for hundreds of years in the form of Operations Research. Prescriptive Analytics has been considered the next step towards increasing data analytics maturity and leading to optimized, ahead-of-time decision-making for business performance improvement. New Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), such as the Internet of Things (IoT), real-time streaming, and sensor-driven business operations, have bolstered prescriptive analytics and provided businesses with accurate prescriptions, facilitating reliable and effective decision-making. Please Consider Your Environmental Responsibilities Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHONOLOGY AND SCIENCE, PILANI Pilani Campus Prescriptive analytics assists the decision-maker in identifying the best action (optimal solution) given the problem context. The difference between decisions made using descriptive/predictive analytics and prescriptive analytics is that a prescriptive analytics algorithm seeks the best decision (optimal solution) based on an objective function (sometimes multiple objective functions) and a set of constraints. Prescriptive analytics models attempt to solve complex optimization problems of the modern era. Students will be exposed to a powerful optimization software package, Lingo, so they can formulate and solve real-life Prescriptive Analytics problems. Students can download a trial version (free) of Lingo from https://www.lindo.com/index.php/products/lingo-and-optimization-modeling Using Lingo, large-scale, complex Prescriptive Analytics problems can be solved. 2. Course Learning Outcomes: a. Students will be able to formulate prescriptive analytics real-life problems and use their applications. b. Students will learn the basics of Linear Programming, Transportation and Assignment problems, Integer Programming, Waiting Line Problems, Simulation modeling, and Goal Programming c. Students will be able to formulate real-life large-sized problems in Lingo software and solve them. They will also learn how to interpret Lingo results and apply them to real-world decision- making for prescriptive analytics problems. 3. Textbooks and References: a. TB1. Taylor, Bernard W.; Introduction to Management Science, Pearson Education, India. 9th Edition or above. b. TB2. Render, B., Stair, Jr., R.M., Hanna, M.E., and Badri, T.N.; Quantitative Analysis for Management, Pearson Education, India, 10th Edition or above. c. RB1. Frederick S. Hillier and Mark S. Course No.: MPBA G524 Course Title: MARKETING ANALYTICS Course Instructors: Prof. Achint Nigam (achint.nigam@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Course Description (Scope and Objective): This course equips students with the analytical frameworks, methods, and tools needed to make evidence-based marketing decisions across the customer lifecycle. It introduces the role of marketing analytics in supporting strategic and operational decisions, distinguishing business intelligence, analytics, and data science, and communicating insights through dashboards and data-driven storytelling. Students will apply analytical techniques to core marketing problems including customer segmentation and positioning, product and pricing analytics, market mix modeling, customer journey analysis, customer experience, retention and lifetime value, digital marketing measurement, and attribution. The course covers methods such as cluster analysis, multidimensional scaling, conjoint analysis, regression, price elasticity modeling, forecasting and diffusion models, principal component analysis, logistic regression, A/B testing, ANOVA, Bayesian networks, and optimization. The course also examines the growing role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, text and image analytics, recommender systems, personalization, and responsible generative AI in marketing. Emphasis is placed on practical interpretation and managerial application of results using tools such as Microsoft Excel, Power BI, DAX, and Python/R. By the end of the course, students will be able to translate marketing data into actionable insights, evaluate marketing performance, and develop data-informed recommendations for products, customers, channels, and brands. Scope of the Course: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of financial derivatives and their applications in managing financial risk. It covers the basic concepts of forwards, futures, options, and swaps, along with their trading mechanisms, pricing principles, and hedging strategies. Students will also gain an introductory understanding of option pricing models, including the Binomial and Black–Scholes models, and explore the use of derivative instruments in equity, currency, interest rate, and fixed-income markets. 2. Course No. : MPBA G532 Course Title : Financial Modelling and Valuation Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Saurabh Chadha (Dept. of Management) 1. Scope and Objectives of the Course: A key component of financial management is the act of calculating and managing a company's value. In essence, managers work to increase the value of their companies in two ways: by increasing the firm's productivity through internal (or organic) growth and by making wise acquisitions that play to the company's core competencies. It follows that practically every significant business choice is decided by asking, "What is it worth?" This course's main goal is to arm you with the conceptual foundation, logical framework, and intuitive reasoning needed to make thoughtful decisions on company value. This course's emphasis is on asses ing the value of the entire enterprise and valuing stock in a company. For our study, we'll depend on the income and market approaches of financial valuation. The course begins by presenting a brief framework on the rules regulating financial statements and changes that are frequently needed to capture the underlying company reality because financial statements serve as the foundation for all types of valuation methodologies. We will use spreadsheet for building the financial model of a company. This course will be most helpful to students who are either pursuing a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting or who would like to do so. The course also has a broader appeal to people who want to improve their Pilani Campus InstructionDivision knowledge of financial analysis and discover how companies produce and quantify value for theirinvestors. 2. Format: This is a fairly challenging and ambitious course by design. We will use case studies and problem-solving techniques because the course objectives are grounded on the practical application of academic ideas. There will be lectures and discussions throughout class time. The readings will be integrated into the lectures' analytic principles, which will provide a helpful framework for a deeper comprehension of the instances. Please keep in mind that the goal of a valuation exercise is to use a series of techniques and logical steps that represent the complexityof thesituation,notto get it "precise." 3. Course No. : MPBA G534 Course Title : People Analytics Instructor-in-charge : MOHAMMAD FARAZ NAIM 1. Course description: There will be three weekly classes. Class time will be devoted to lectures, role-plays, exercises, questionnaire, case discussions and videotapes. Lectures will provide analytical concepts that will integrate the readings and serve as useful framework for a richer understanding of cases and role-plays. Role-plays, cases and videotapes provide the "application" aspects of this course. These participative activities are further enhanced by rigorous self-review (through Journal, Follow-up Report and Critique). Tests and Project will provide an opportunity to test comprehension of the theory and readings. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: People Analytics is the application of data science and information technology in the domain of Human resource management. The present course is designed to progress the understanding of the role of data-driven decisions about people's issues in an organization. This emerging discipline signifies the strategic role of HR function in the contemporary organizations. However, with the advent of analytics, it has evolved into a holistic function taking care of all people related aspects at the workplace, not only traditional HR operations. It serves as a key driver in pursuit of sustainable competitive advantage for organizations by leveraging data driven practices for an improved decision making. Grounded on 4Ts principle: Task, Theory, Technique, and Technology; the course integrates underlying theories and principles, and data analytical tools and techniques to drive business objectives. The course is structured to equip students with hands-on experience on analytical softwares to track, maintain, retrieve, analyze, and interpret HR data (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information) to contribute to business outcomes. This will serve the twin purpose of elevating the students’ understanding on nuances of analytics in organizations, which will aid in students’ value addition and employability. The learning objectives of the course are as under:  This course introduces the student to the theory, concepts, and business application of human resources research, data, metrics, systems, analyses, and reporting. _ Pilani Campus Instruction Division  The student will develop an understanding of the role and importance of HR analytics, and the ability to track, store, retrieve, analyze and interpret HR data to support decision making.  The student will know about the standard HR metrics to measure various facets of HR related outputs and about indices and metrics to measure them.  Employ appropriate software to record, maintain, retrieve and analyze human resources information (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information).  Apply quantitative and qualitative analysis to understand trends and indicators in human resource data; understand and apply various statistical analysis methods.  Apply descriptive and predictive analytics techniques to address HR related issues and make data driven decision making.  Demonstrate how to connect HR results to business results. 3. Course Description: Basic techniques of pharmaceutical analysis, data handling and analysis, sources of error in analysis. The analytical methods would comprise various titrimetric methods, such as acid-base, complexometric, non-aqueous, oxidation-reduction, precipitation, conductometric; physical and instrumental analysis such as gravimetric, polarography, nephelometry, amperometry, turbidometry, potentiometry; chromatographic separations such as TLC, column, ion-exchange, extraction methods such as gel-filtration, fractionation processes, analysis of metallic and non-metallic elements; water content, as well as evaluation of drug constituents in various pharmaceutical preparation. 2. Course Description: This course is a laboratory oriented course and covers instrumentation and applications of various analytical techniques such as UV-visible, Infrared, NMR spectroscopy, Mass spectrometry etc for drug discovery and development 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The course is aimed at exposing the students to modern analytical techniques in relevance to pharmaceutical industries. Course Number : PHA F315 Course Title : PHARMACEUTICAL FORMULATIONS II Instructor-in-charge : Ankit Jain (ankit.j@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in, 3170-M) Lab Instructors : Sweta Acharya, Yash Patidar, Yashika Tomar, Vagesh Verma, Shivangi Nema, Kumbhar Pragati Ramesh, Desai Vaibhavi Meghraj 1. Course description: Physical, chemical, and biopharmaceutical considerations in formulations, absorption, distribution, and elimination of drugs; pharmaceutical additives; formulation, manufacturing, packaging, quality control, and stability of solid dosage forms, semi-solid dosage forms, liquids dosage forms, and sterile preparations including parenteral suspensions, emulsions, depot formulations; microencapsulation and controlled release formulations; targeted drug delivery systems; multi-unit particulate systems; transdermal, gastroretentive, and nasopulmonary drug delivery systems; aerosol products and packaging. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: It is a course intended to give students insight into the problems involved in making drug dosage forms. It brings together the various sciences involved in developing pharmaceutical product formulations and evaluating their quality. The laboratory component involves some fundamental exercises in the evolution of products such as tablets, ointments, solutions, parenteral products, sustained-action medications, etc. It also imparts knowledge of newer dosage forms. 3. Course learning outcomes: CLO1. Explain the principles of preformulation, formulation, manufacturing, packaging, quality control, and stability of conventional pharmaceutical dosage forms, including solid, liquid, semi-solid, and sterile preparations. CLO2. Apply pharmaceutical formulation principles and standard manufacturing techniques to prepare and evaluate conventional and modified-release dosage forms, while adhering to Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) and quality requirements. CLO3. Compare and evaluate the design, advantages, limitations, and pharmaceutical applications of novel drug delivery systems, including controlled-release, targeted, transdermal, gastroretentive, multiparticulate, nasopulmonary, and aerosol dosage forms. 4. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course covers key immunologic concepts: how the components of the immune system are generated, organized, and function; the mechanisms that lead to beneficial immune responses, immune disorders, and immunodeficiencies; methods to identify immune reactions; and ways to manipulate the immune system and its components to benefit the patient. Course Description: Overview of new drug research and development; Bioethics and institutional review board; regulatory control of clinical trials for NDA & ANDA application; Good Clinical Practice (GCP); related ICH guidelines; applied clinical epidemiology and biostatistics; clinical trial study design; trial development (protocol, case report form, and data management); clinical trial management- coordinating clinical trial at the site, documentation methodology, implementing monitoring plan and performing quality control; statistical analysis and data interpretation; monitoring obligations and methods; and Medical writing & report preparation for various submissions. 2. Course Description: This course deals with the strategy and tactics involved in the synthesis of organic molecules. The idea is to identify key structural features in the target molecules and then go backward logically to identify appropriate starting materials and chemical reactions for their synthesis. Knowledge and understanding of common organic reagents and reaction mechanisms are required for this course. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: Most life-saving drugs are organic molecules. This course aims to develop a logical understanding which can be used to propose the synthesis of an organic compound. This course teaches various strategies and tactics together with the common nomenclature used in Retrosynthetic Analysis. At the end of the course, students should be able to propose a synthetic scheme for various drug molecules with appropriate justification. 3. Course Number : PHY F211 Course Title : Classical Mechanics Instructor-in-Charge : Biswanath Layek (layek@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in; 3242-B) Course Description: This course introduces the principles of classical mechanics from Newtonian and analytical perspectives. It covers constrained motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, variational principles, central-force dynamics, canonical transformations, Poisson brackets, the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies in inertial, and rotating reference frames. Scope & Objectives: To provide a strong foundation in analytical mechanics and equip students with the mathematical and physical tools required to formulate, analyze, and solve problems in classical mechanics with elegance and rigor. Importantly, the course serves as a gateway to advanced topics in theoretical physics, including quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, electrodynamics, and general relativity. Course learning outcomes:  Apply vector calculus, generalized coordinates, and analytical methods to formulate and solve problems involving the motion of particles and systems with constraints using Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations.  Analyze central-force motion and variational principles to derive equations of motion, identify conserved quantities, investigate orbital dynamics and stability, and explain the role of symmetries in classical mechanics.  Employ Hamiltonian mechanics, canonical transformations, generating functions, and Poisson brackets to transform, simplify, and solve dynamical systems while recognizing canonical invariants.  Evaluate the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies using orthogonal transformations, Euler angles, and rotating reference frames, including the analysis of Coriolis and related (non) inertial effects. Text Books: T1. H. Goldstein, C. Poole, and J. Safko, Classical Mechanics, Third Edition, Pearson Edu. Inc., 2002. T2. N. C. Rana and P. S. Course No ​​ : PHY F312 Course Title ​ ​ : STATISTICAL MECHANICS Instructor-in-Charge​ : Tapomoy Guha Sarkar Instructor: Tapomoy Guha Sarkar 1. Course Description: This is a first course on Statistical mechanics aimed at students who have familiarity with classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and classical thermodynamics. The stress is on developing the essential techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics for non-interacting systems. Classical Thermodynamics, as a study of macroscopic properties of materials, is no doubt an incredibly elegant interface between us and nature. Historically born out of the remarkable power of empiricism in the nineteenth century, the laws of Thermodynamics have stood the test of time. In its breadth of generality and profundity, the subject has found applications in almost all areas of fundamental and applied sciences. Here, we must note that scientific pedagogy is not necessarily chronologically ordered. The fast development in our understanding of matter at the microscopic level through advances in the atomic theories in the twentieth century required classical thermodynamics to find reconciliation with physics at the microscopic level. The role of statistics in bridging the laws of mechanics with those of thermodynamics is probably as profound as the laws themselves. In a first course on statistical mechanics aimed towards a target audience comprising undergraduate students of basic sciences and engineering it is important to reveal the subject in its broad, multi-layered beauty. The course aims to look at Thermodynamics as an emergent phenomenon and emphasize the role of statistics in bridging the microscopic and macroscopic descriptions. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: ❖​ Develop familiarity with the basic techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics. ❖​ Understand the role of probability theory and statistics in relating microscopic and macroscopic descriptions of thermodynamic systems ❖​ Learn key methods of ensemble theory ❖​ Distinguish between quantum and classical statistical mechanics and compute essential properties of ideal Bosonic and Fermionic systems. 3. Course No: PHY F413 Course Title : Particle Physics Instructor-in-Charge: Rishikesh Vaidya Instructor(s): NA Tutorial/Practical Instructors: NA 1. Course Description: (Just as every book has a preface, I will avail this space to elaborate about the course in great detail. It will be a synopsis of particle physics, providing context for the questions it addresses and a sense of the answers that will be discussed in the course. Hopefully, it will give you a fair idea of what particle physics is all about and what to expect from this course. The titles of paragraphs may seem out of place or even nonsensical in the first reading. Some things will fall in place as you read through the handout. For some other stuff, you may have to wait till the end of the course.) Bright blue sky: What are the most fundamental questions we can pose in Physics? 1. What are the most fundamental building blocks (called particles for the want of a better word) of the Universe? 2. What are the fundamental forces (interaction is a better word) that bind them to form the structural hierarchy we see at different levels? 3. What can we know about the particles and their dynamics if we know the answers to the above questions? 4. Are there fundamental principles that mandate the existence of different kinds of fundamental particles and different kinds of fundamental interactions? Is there an overarching theme in the answers we know? Particle Physics aims to offer concrete answers to the above questions, though some caveats remain. Our present understanding of these questions is summarised in the so-called Standard Model (SM) of Particle Physics. This course will offer some answers within the framework of the Standard Model of Particle Physics. Relativity + Quantum Mechanics = Quantum Field Theory: Before I give a glimpse of answers to the above questions, we must ask for the framework for particle physics. It turns out that the natural framework for particle physics is a quantum theory for a system of fields. Let us understand the reason behind this. We will be talking about the most fundamental particles and their interactions at the minutest length scales, so quantum mechanics is inescapable. To study smaller and smaller length scales, we need probes whose wavelengths are sufficiently small. Thus, we use extremely high-energy particles (relativistic velocities imply larger momentum and hence smaller wavelengths). Hence, special relativity is a must. How about the study of mesons (bound states of quarks-antiquarks) and 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division baryons (bound states of three quarks)? Here again, surprisingly, it is quantum mechanics that ensures relativistic conditions. Whenever you confine a quantum system to a tiny volume, uncertainties in the momenta become extremely large, implying relativistic conditions. Thus, quarks inside protons and neutrons are quite hot and hence relativistic. Now, under relativistic conditions, you can literally "cook" an arbitrarily large number of particles-antiparticle pairs, if you pump in a sufficient amount of energy. Thus, your underlying dynamical system must be inherently capable of describing situations involving an arbitrarily large number of particles. Thus, any framework with a fixed number of particles is doomed to fail. A system of fields with infinitely many degrees of freedom is the right dynamical system to describe relativistic interactions. Thus, relativity + quantum mechanics = Quantum Field Theory. Quantum Field Theory is demanding, and a typical graduate school has at least two courses in Quantum Field Theory before one can survey any literature in Particle Physics. However, the purpose of any undergraduate course in particle physics is essentially twofold: a) to provide a glimpse of the power of symmetry principles in the origin and classification of fundamental particles and their interactions, and b) to demonstrate the power of perturbative calculations of scattering cross-sections and decay rates via Feynman rules. To meet this end, we will follow an approach pioneered by Richard Feynman. This is the structure and approach of a first course in particle physics worldwide. It is just not possible to do squeeze in relativistic quantum field theory and particle physics in one semester, without any prior exposure to either of them. From relativistic quantum mechanics to scattering cross-sections and decay rate: Answers to questions 1 and 2 have been the content of the latter half of your Nuclear and Particle Physics course. The focus of this course would be essentially on questions 3 and 4. It turns out that we know a lot about the fundamental particles and their interactions. In the first module, we will primarily focus on calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates. To do this, we will quickly recap the special theory of relativity (module 1) and the time-dependent perturbation theory (module 2). In Module 2, we will also discuss the relativistic quantum mechanics of spin-0 particles (the Klein-Gordon equation). Module-3 will introduce spin-1/2 particles (Dirac equation) and apply them to classic scattering cross-section calculations in quantum electrodynamics at lowest order in perturbation theory. You will see the famous Feynman diagrams and Feynman rules in action.. We will have some fun with what one can do with the rules, and that is calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates, which experimentalists can actually measure. Course No : PHY F422 Course Title : Group Theory and Applications Instructor-in-Charge : Bhavesh Chauhan 1. Course Description: This is an introductory course on Group Theory, designed for undergraduates and PhD scholars, with an emphasis on applications in physics. Many physical systems exhibit symmetry, which allows for a simplified analysis. The mathematical language of describing and studying a vast class of these symmetries is Group Theory. In each case, the symmetry operations are represented by individual group elements and their combinations. Discrete symmetries entail discrete groups, which may contain a finite or infinite number of elements. Continuous symmetries entail continuous groups (also called as ‘Lie groups’). In this course, we will cover the structure, classification, and representations of groups. We will see how group theory can help us understands some aspects of quantum mechanics, classical mechanics, and most importantly, particle interactions. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: • Identify and classify discrete and continuous symmetries in physical systems using the foundational concepts of group theory. • Apply the principles of representation theory to decompose group representations into irreducible components and interpret their physical significance. • Demonstrate the application of group theory in quantum mechanics by analyzing the symmetry structure of the hydrogen atom and explaining the role of conserved quantities and degeneracies. • Analyze physical systems under spacetime symmetry transformations using continuous groups such as the Lorentz and Poincaré groups. • Analyze particle interactions and fundamental forces using the mathematical framework of Lie groups and Lie algebras. 3. topics_text: Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division FIRST SEMESTER 2026-27 Course Handout Classical and Quantum Waves Date: 1.08.2026 In addition to part I (the General Handout for all courses, appended to the Time table), this section provides further specific details regarding the course. Course Number: PHY U101 Course Title: Classical and Quantum Waves Instructor-in-Charge: Kaushar Vaidya Instructors: Anshuman Dalvi, Raj Kumar Gupta, Tapomoy Guha Sarkar, Kaushar Vaidya Tutorial Instructors: Debasish Bandyopadhyay, Arpan Das, Amol Holkundkar, Tanmoy Mondal, Sajal Mukherjee, D. D. Pant, Niladri Sarkar, Kaushar Vaidya 1. Course Description: This course takes us from the study of oscillations to waves, and finally to the foundations of quantum mechanics, tracing a connected thread through classical and modern physics. We begin with an introduction to oscillations and the model of simple harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, leading to the phenomenon of resonance. We shall study coupled oscillators: normal modes and frequencies, and the continuum limit of a large number of coupled oscillators. We will study transverse vibrations of a stretched string, the one-dimensional wave equation, and traveling wave solutions to the wave equation. We shall study energy transport in waves and pulses on a string, and their interaction with a boundary: reflection and refraction. Wave phenomena, such as the interference of light waves from two coherent sources, will lead us to wave-particle duality, the concept of the photon, the de Broglie hypothesis, and matter waves. We shall study the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, and the wavefunction. We shall study the quantum problem of a particle in a one-dimensional box, energy quantization, barrier tunneling, the transmission coefficient, and introduce scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of quantum tunneling. 2. Course No : PHY U102 Course Title : Introduction to Classical and Quantum Waves Instructor-in-Charge : Madhukar Mishra 1. Course Description: Introduction to oscillations, simple harmonic motion, superposition of harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, resonance and quality factor: transverse and longitudinal waves, wave speed in a stretched string, wave equation in one dimension, traveling solutions to the wave equation, energy transport in waves, standing waves, travelling sound waves; Interference of light waves, introduction to diffraction; concept of photon, photoelectric effect, Compton scattering; wave-particle duality, de Broglie hypothesis and matter waves; 1D Quantum wave functions: properties and applications; Pauli’s exclusion principle and multielectrons atoms, introduction to X-rays and Lasers. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of classical and quantum waves, beginning with simple harmonic motion as the basis of oscillatory phenomena and progressing through mechanical waves, sound, interference, and diffraction. It then explores the transition from classical to quantum physics by examining the wave-particle nature of light and matter, culminating in an elementary introduction to quantum wave functions and their applications to atomic systems, X-rays, and lasers. Designed for undergraduate students with a basic knowledge of calculus, the course emphasizes physical intuition, conceptual understanding, and qualitative reasoning over advanced mathematical formalism. Its objective is to provide a unified understanding of wave phenomena across classical and quantum physics, establish the conceptual foundations of modern physics, and prepare students for advanced courses in optics, quantum mechanics, condensed matter physics, and related disciplines. 3. Textbooks: (i) Principles of Physics (10th Edition) by Halliday, Resnick, and Walker, John Wiley & Sons. (T.B.) 4. Reference Books: (i) Physics, Vols. 1 & 2, by Halliday, Resnick, & Krane, 5th Ed., John Wiley & Sons. 2002. (ii) Berkeley Physics Course, Vol. 3, Waves, by Frank S. Crawford Jr, Special Indian Edition, McGraw-Hill, 2011. (iii) Fundamentals of Optics, Fourth International Edition, Jenkins & White, McGraw-Hill, 1981. (iv) Concepts of Modern Physics, 7th Edition, Arthur Beiser, McGraw-Hill, 2017 5. Course Learning Outcomes: (i) Explain the principles of simple harmonic motion and analyze damped and forced oscillations, resonance, and the superposition of oscillatory motion as the foundation of wave phenomena. 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division (ii) Describe the behavior of classical waves, including wave propagation, wave equations, energy transport, sound waves, and the formation of standing waves in one-dimensional systems. (iii) Explain the wave nature of light through interference and diffraction and discuss the experimental observations that established the quantum nature of light, including the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering. (iv) Describe the concept of matter waves by explaining wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and the extension of wave concepts from light to material particles. (v) Interpret the physical meaning of quantum wave functions in one dimension and explain their role in describing quantum systems, including an introductory understanding of multi-electron atoms through Pauli's exclusion principle and the principles of X-rays and lasers. 6. Course No : SNS F211 Course Title : Fundamentals of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology Instructor-in-Charge : Prof. Sarbani Ghosh (sarbani.ghosh@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) Class Timings : M W 5 Th 10 Hour 1. Course Description: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered. 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field. 3. Course Learning Outcomes: After successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: 1 Pilani Campus ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION ◦ Explain the fundamental principles of nanoscience, including size-dependent properties and quantum effects at the nanoscale. ◦ Describe and compare common synthesis techniques used for nanomaterials. ◦ Analyze the structure–property–application relationships of nanomaterials in areas such as electronics, energy, catalysis, and biomedical systems. 4. Course No : SNS F214 Course Title : Fundamentals of Solid-State Physics Instructor-in-Charge : Jayendra N. Bandyopadhyay 1. Course Description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental concepts of solid-state physics with a particular emphasis on semiconductor materials and their applications. It covers crystal structures and defects, the quantum and statistical principles governing electron behavior in solids, the origin of energy bands, and the electronic properties of metals, semiconductors, and insulators. The course further introduces carrier transport mechanisms, including drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect, before discussing the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids. Throughout the course, the underlying physical principles are connected to modern semiconductor devices such as LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, and sensors, providing students with the essential foundation required for advanced studies in materials science, condensed matter physics, and semiconductor technology. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: This course introduces the fundamental principles of solid-state physics that underpin the behavior of crystalline materials and modern semiconductor devices. It encompasses crystal structures, basic quantum and statistical concepts, electronic band theory, semiconductor physics, and the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids, while emphasizing their relevance to contemporary electronic and optoelectronic technologies. The primary objective is to develop a clear understanding of the relationship between the atomic structure of solids and their physical properties, explain the quantum mechanical origin of electronic behavior in materials, introduce the principles governing charge transport in semiconductors, and establish the scientific foundation necessary for the study, analysis, and application of semiconductor materials and devices in advanced engineering and physics courses. 3. Course Learning Outcomes: (i) Describe crystal structures, Bravais lattices, crystal systems, common crystal structures, and Miller indices, and explain their significance in determining the physical properties of crystalline solids. (ii) Apply the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics to explain wave-particle duality, quantized energy levels, and the origin of electronic states in solids. (iii) Differentiate between Maxwell–Boltzmann, Bose–Einstein, and Fermi–Dirac statistics, and explain the statistical behavior of electrons and other particles in solids. (iv) Explain electrical conduction in solids using the Drude model and band theory, and relate density of states and effective mass to the electronic properties of materials. (v) Analyze the electrical properties of intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors and explain carrier transport through drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect. 1 Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division (vi) Explain the thermal and magnetic properties of solids in terms of lattice vibrations, phonons, heat capacity, and magnetic ordering. (vii) Explain the optical properties of semiconductors and relate them to the operation of optoelectronic devices, including LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, and semiconductor sensors. 4. Course No : SS G562 Course Title : SOFTWARE ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT Instructor-in-Charge : Dr. Tanmaya Mahapatra (Email: tanmaya.mahapatra@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) 1. Course Description: Software engineering is a discipline that allows us to apply engineering and computer science con- cepts in the development and maintenance of reliable, usable, and dependable software. There are several areas to focus on within software engineering, such as requirement specification, de- sign, development, testing, maintenance and project management. Software development outside of the classroom is a very complex process, mostly because real-world software is much larger and more complex. The purpose of this course is to present software engineering as a body of knowledge. The course is designed to present software engineering concepts and principles in parallel with the software development life cycle. 2. Scope & Objective of the Course: This course provides an ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex engineering problems by applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics. This also develops an ability to function effectively in a team whose members together provide leadership, create a collaborative and inclusive environment, establish goals, plan tasks, and meet objectives. In addition, this course also facilitates an ability to develop and conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze and interpret data, and use engineering judgment to draw conclusions 3. Learning Outcomes Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: • Understand and apply fundamental software engineering principles throughout the software development life cycle. • Identify, formulate, and solve complex software engineering problems using appropriate en- gineering, scientific, and mathematical principles. • Elicit, specify, and analyze software requirements for real-world systems. • Design structured, modular, and maintainable software systems. • Develop, test, and maintain software using modern tools and best practices. 1 • Function effectively as a member or leader of a diverse team, demonstrating collaboration and project management skills. • Plan and manage software projects, including task estimation, scheduling, and risk analysis. • Demonstrate awareness of ethical, legal, and societal issues in software engineering. 4. Textbooks: TB1. Software Engineering, Sommerville I., 10th , Pearson Education, 2010. TB2. Software Engineering: A Practitioner’s Approach, Pressman, R.S., McGraw Hill Inter- national Edition, 2010. References: Ref1. An Integrated Approach to Software Engineering, Jalote, P., 2nd Edition, Narosa, 1998. Ref2. Software Engineering, Schach, S., Tata MCgraw Hill, 7th Ed., 2007. Ref3. Software Engineering Fundamentals, Behforooz, A. & F.J. Hudson, OUP, 2006. Ref4. Foundations of Software Engineering, Ahmed A, CRC Press, 2016. Additional Readings as assigned and/or made available online by the I/C. 5.
